articles.title: 'They're not done': Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison says AI can finally help us 'finish' building apps, dismissing SaaSpocalypse fears
articles.content: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison has pushed back at the suggestion that artificial intelligence could end software and SaaS businesses like his, arguing that AI will actually just make enterprise applications even more capable than they ever have been. Speaking during his keynote at the company's annual AI World conference, Ellison directly addressed ongoing concerns that businesses could use AI to build their own software – we've already seen many popular apps and suites like Adobe's Creative Cloud be imitated by AI, for example. "There's been some talk about there's going to be a SaaSpocalypse because everyone's going to use AI to build their own applications," he said. "I don't think that's quite true. I think companies will continue to build applications, but they will be quite different because of AI." Future apps will be fully tailored to geographies and industries Rather than making today's software redundant, Ellison believes AI will allow developers to make their apps far more comprehensive, capable of handling entire business processes and fine-tuned for every type of sector and business need. He argued that even the most established enterprise applications today are only so good, automating just a proportion of the processes businesses actually need. "They may be the best things that are commercially available... [but] they're not done," he revealed, acknowledging that many sectors still need to build their own extensions and buy other third-party apps and connectors. "For the first time... [the] software industry can actually finish the applications if we start doing them industry by industry." Oracle's biggest clear push is in the healthcare sector currently, with Ellison speaking on stage about the notoriously complex and highly regulated nature of this industry – immense challenges for one global software company when navigating endless geographical variabilities is a must. SaaSpocalypse doesn't kill off apps – but it certainly shifts the focus from interface to functionality Ellison also believes that AI could fundamentally change how workers interact with applications, replacing complicated menus, dashboards and multi-step processes with smoother, natural language interaction. "If you can ask a question describing what you want to see, you should then immediately see it. Any other user interface is nonsense." "There should be no training required to use any of these applications," he added. While Ellison remains confident about the future of commercial software, that doesn't necessarily mean businesses will continue to interact with apps in the same way, and it seems that a company as big as Oracle is singing from the same hymn sheet. In two separate interviews with TechRadar Pro , company execs pointed toward the same trend. Brian Chess, NetSuite's Chief Operating Officer, implied that the underlying business software could eventually become invisible to users. Discussing customers who might prefer to access NetSuite through AI assistants like ChatGPT or other platforms like Slack, Chess said "If they never log in, that's ok with us." Oracle knows that as long as it can still serve as a company's system of record, adapting to new ways of access is a must. But what this means is that, for software vendors, the value of their products will likely come more from the data, logic and processes they manage, rather than the polished interface they've been used to building for potentially decades. Ultimately, earlier SaaSpocalypse concerns remain valid, but it's not so much about AI wiping software from the world entirely. It just marks the next chapter in software, where interfaces become less critical and functionality becomes the biggest USP. Shares in Oracle rose around 14% to $144.14 in the couple of days that Oracle AI World took place, likely partly in thanks to Ellison's thoughts on the future of software as well as the company's whole suite of product announcements, but share prices are still down markedly…

articles.title: LG C6 vs Samsung S90H: which of these 2026 OLED TVs comes out on top?
articles.content: The LG C6 is easily one of the best TVs I’ve tested this year, showing a significant upgrade over its predecessor, the LG C5. The new model has faster performance, a real step-up in brightness (nearly 300 nits peak HDR and 50 fullscreen HDR) and a more accurate picture, especially with its color temperature, mitigating some of the green tint I saw in the LG C5 when I compared the C6 and C5 side-by-side . While the LG C6 does currently sit at the top of the TV food chain for me, in terms of performance vs price, there are some rivals I’ve been intrigued to test alongside it. One of those has just landed in our testing lab: the Samsung S90H, Samsung’s own mid-range OLED and direct rival to the C6. I decided to compare the two side-by-side using reference 4K Blu-ray scenes I use to test TVs. Can the S90H cement itself as one of the best OLED TVs and de-throne the LG C6? Brightness and bright room viewing Despite the S90H (right) having higher measured brightness, this scene from Lawrence of Arabia looked brighter on the C6 (left) (Image credit: Sony Picture Entertainment / Future ) In terms of brightness measurements, the C6 registered 1,427 nits peak HDR brightness in Filmmaker Mode, which is a nice result for a mid-range OLED. Surprisingly, the S90H measured 1,689 nits peak HDR brightness in its own Filmmaker Mode, which is 18% higher than the C6. Samsung’s OLED TVs are brighter than LG’s, with the Samsung S95H/S99H flagship OLED registering 10% higher brightness than the LG G6 in HDR Filmmaker Mode (2,739 nits for the S95H/S99H vs 2,475 nits for the G6). The S90H’s fullscreen HDR brightness was also higher, measuring 310 nits to the C6’s 247 nits, both of which were measured in Filmmaker Mode. So, with measurements, the S90H is brighter. But, did this translate across to real-world viewing? Firing up Lawrence of Arabia , focusing on a bright, daytime desert scene early in the movie, the C6 actually showed higher luminance. The white sands appeared punchier and brighter on the C6 compared to the S90H. This was the case with both TVs in Filmmaker Mode and even in the brighter Movie mode (called Cinema Home on the C6). In fact, the perceived brightness gap was even wider when set to their movie modes, with the C6 rendering the white sands and blue skies even brighter. When it comes to bright room viewing, the S90H (right) is the obvious choice, thanks to its glare free screen (Image credit: Warner Bros / Future ) This could be a result of the C6’s new Alpha 11 AI Gen 3 processor, the same used in the flagship G6, which does feature an impressive brightness booster and 13-bit color processing (12-bit with 1 bit of added brightness), as well as the C6’s glossy screen vs the S90H’s matte screen. It wasn’t all cut-and-dry, as in some scenes, particularly colorful ones, the S90H looked punchier at times (I’ll get onto that in the below Color section). One thing is for sure though: for bright room viewing, the S90H is the clear victor. The C6’s reflective screen was one of its negatives in my C6 review, often showing mirror-like reflections during darker scenes. The S90H features Samsung’s OLED Glare Free screen and as expected, it’s super effective at eliminating these reflections. I used dark scenes from movies like The Batman and Project Hail Mary to really test it out, and I was surprised by how well the S90H displayed these scenes in our bright testing lab. If you have a bright room, the S90H is the better choice. Colors Colors are excellent on both TVs, but they often trade off whose is punchier. In The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, it's the C6 (left)... Nintendo / Universal Pictures / Future ...But in Speed Racer, it's the S90H (right) Warner Bros / Future Color is probably the toughest battle fought between these two TVs. Watching The Super Mario Galaxy Movie , both TVs did a great job faithfully recreating the movie’s bright and vivid colors. In a scene where the Lumas gather for story time at the start of the movie, their…

articles.title: DJI brought drone navigation to your floors with the Romo P — our Home Device of the Year
articles.content: The Romo P is DJI’s first foray into the world of floor-cleaning, and the company's years of expertise in navigation and obstacle-detection have translated flawlessly from the sky to your floor. The most important aspect of a robot vacuum, though, is its cleaning ability, and in our tests the Romo P more than holds its own against established leaders like Roborock and Dreame — read our in-depth DJI Romo P review for more. It’s a hugely impressive package all-round, and my choice for Home Device of the Year in TechRadar's Product of the Year Awards 2026 . DJI’s drones have offered autonomous navigation since 2016, and it's that expertise that gives the Romo P the edge when it comes to pathfinding. It combines dual fisheye cameras with LiDAR to detect objects as small as 2mm thick (that's less than an eighth of an inch), so there’s no need to worry about cables or shoelaces getting wrapped around the brushroll. The Romo P packs serious cleaning power inside its space-age chassis too, tackling dirt, dust and pet hair across all floor types. With 25,000Pa suction and extendable cleaning brushes, it’s particularly well suited to wood, tiles and other hard surfaces, and it’s no slouch on carpet either, easily keeping up with rival robovacs. (Image credit: Future) Wet cleaning is especially impressive; the Romo P’s dual mop heads are noticeably more plush and absorbent than those of other robovacs we’ve tested, and the right-hand head articulates out slightly to clean all the way to the edge of furniture and baseboards without leaving dust lines (a common issue with round robovacs). When it needs to move onto carpet, the mop heads raise automatically to keep the floor dry. Once the Romo P has finished cleaning, its automated charging and self-cleaning dock takes over. This surprisingly compact unit sucks dirt from the romovac’s bin into a sealed dust bag to keep dirt and allergens safely contained, then washes the mop pads and dries them to prevent mold and odors. The process is so effective that you might only need to intervene a few times a year. The Romo P is controlled via DJI’s Home app, which lets you customize its automated functions to suit your floors and lifestyle. For example, you can set up custom cleaning schedules, and adjust the Romo P’s suction and mopping-water levels on a room-by-room basis. Like any good robovac app, DJI Home also allows you to set no-go zones, and monitor cleaning progress in real time. (Image credit: Future) That’s not all — the app also gives you a ground-level view of your room via the robot’s two fish-eye camera lenses, so you can, for example, check on your pets while you’re away. There's full voice control too. The Romo P is even a cut above other robot vacuums when it comes to aesthetics, with its transparent top panel and matching see-through dock letting you see exactly what’s happening while the duo keep your home spotless with little-and-often cleaning. They’re a far cry from the usual black or white pucks and chunky docks of most robovacs. DJI has launched itself into your home in style, with a robot vacuum that can literally run rings around its competitors, and its Romo P is a thoroughly worthy winner of our Home Device of the Year award.

articles.title: NASA Seeks Proposals for Reboosting the Hubble Space Telescope
articles.content: The Hubble Space Telescope "will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s," reports Ars Technica. So now NASA has released a Request For Information (RFI) "asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble." Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. "The requirement includes that the boost and/or servicing mission must not harm the HST and that this mission is expected to occur by 2032," NASA wrote in the RFI. The contractor would be responsible for providing the launch vehicle, servicing spacecraft, mission operations, and "crew if applicable." NASA is not committing to buying a Hubble rescue mission, but officials want to know who might be interested in mounting such a mission, how much it would cost, and which companies would have a realistic shot at reaching Hubble before it falls out of orbit and burns up on reentry. Orbital dynamicists currently predict that it will likely happen in 2033 or 2034 without intervention, but reentry forecasts can change based on solar activity... A reboost to NASA's requirement of 373 miles (600 km) would likely keep Hubble in orbit for at least 25 more years. "NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002," the article points out, "when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission." The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction... NASA's newer flagship observatories, sometimes described as successors to Hubble, are not actually one-for-one replacements. Hubble is tuned to observe the Universe in visible and ultraviolet light, while the Webb and Roman telescopes peer deeper into the infrared Universe. Astronomers will likely have to wait for the launch of NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory in the 2040s for an improvement on Hubble's visible and ultraviolet vision. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: The scariest movies streaming on Netflix, HBO Max, Hulu, and Prime Video to watch this Halloween
articles.content: Looking for a horror movie to watch this Halloween? As a huge horror fan, I've seen a lot of them over the years, and precious few are worth your time. With all the new movies coming and going from the best streaming platforms every month, narrowing down what to watch next can be a little overwhelming. That's where I come in. I'm shining a spotlight on the best horror movies available across all the major streaming platforms, from Netflix and Prime Video to HBO Max and Hulu. Whether you're in the mood for a tried-and-true classic, an underrated gem or a newer release that deserves a spot on your Halloween watchlist, I've got plenty of spooky recommendations to help make your movie night a scream. 'Sinners' (HBO Max) If you're just dipping your toes into the horror genre, this is the one to watch. I recommend "Sinners" to horror fans and non-horror fans alike. Director Ryan Coogler's vampire horror blockbuster feels more like church than a movie; its sound design is so mesmerizing and electric, you can't help but get swept up in the fever. Honestly, maybe it's for the best that I didn't catch this movie in theaters. I'd have been shoutin' down the aisles. Set in 1930s Mississippi, "Sinners" tells the story of twin brothers (both played by long-time Coogler collaborator Michael B. Jordan), who return to their hometown to convert an abandoned sawmill into the juke joint of their dreams. Opening night is a roaring success, until a gang of vampires led by Jack O'Connell's chilling and charming Remmick crashes the party. Watch "Sinners" on HBO Max now 'The Substance' (Hulu) Demi Moore enjoyed a well-deserved career resurgence thanks to her fearless performance in "The Substance," which earned a rare horror movie Best Actress nomination for her portrayal of Elisabeth Sparkle, a fading Hollywood star in her 50s. After being unceremoniously fired by her producer (Dennis Quaid) for being too old, Elisabeth turns to a black-market drug that unleashes a younger, hotter version of herself (Margaret Qualley) to step back into the spotlight she craves. There's just one catch: This substance comes with a strict set of instructions, and failing to follow them can (and does) have some seriously gruesome consequences. A stomach-churning yet remarkably effective satire on how the entertainment industry treats aging women, Coralie Fargeat's "The Substance" is one of the rare body-horror films to win over major awards committees, scoring five Oscar nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director. Watch "The Substance" on Hulu now 'The Witch' (Prime Video) Before Robert Eggers' "Werwulf" comes out this Christmas, you owe it to yourself to catch the horror movie that put him on the map: "The Witch." This 2015 chilling folk horror tale cemented the filmmaker as a talent to watch, and while its slow pacing and old-timey dialogue might be a turn off for some folks, if you're willing to sit with it, I promise you "The Witch" is a horror film you won't soon forget. Set in 17th-century New England, it follows brooding patriarch William (Ralph Ineson) and his family after they’re banished from their settlement and forced to start over on a remote farm bordering a clearly haunted forest. When their youngest son, Samuel, goes missing, their eldest daughter, Thomasin (Anya Taylor-Joy) is the first suspect thanks to her witchy ways. Along with the winter's cold, paranoia sets in, and William grows convinced that something evil is lurking in the woods — and that Thomasin may be to blame. Watch "The Witch" on Prime Video now 'Oculus' (Netflix) Before "Carrie" and "Haunting of Hill House," acclaimed horror director Mike Flanagan provided some nightmare fuel that haunts me to this day with "Oculus." This trippy horror movie adds a fresh perspective to a familiar framework, where a cursed mirror not only warps the minds of the main characters, but disorients the audience until you're questioning what's real and what's a hallucination. Said mirror is…

articles.title: iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: which should you choose?
articles.content: Apple iPhone Duo The iPhone Duo is a phone-and-tablet all-in-one, offering an extra screen at a much higher price than the iPhone 18 Pro. It also loses some key Pro features. Pros Excellent design Two screens Stylus support Cons Very expensive Worse cameras No Face ID Apple iPhone 18 Pro The iPhone 18 Pro is a much cheaper phone than the iPhone Duo, with better cameras to boot. But its single screen makes it far less versatile. Pros Superb cameras Much lower price Has Face ID Cons Just one screen No stylus support Smaller battery The iPhone Duo has been a long time coming, but is Apple’s first foldable a home run? And even if it is, do you even really need a dual-screen device? Those are questions you might be asking yourself if you're in the market for a new iPhone — especially when the iPhone 18 Pro is also available, which only has one display but is a better device in various other ways. So, to help you decide which of these two models is best for you, we’ve compared the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro across various categories, including price, display, and design. Happy decision-making! iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: specs comparison Before we look in depth at the key elements of the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, the specs table below provides an overview of their similarities and differences. iPhone Duo iPhone 18 Pro Dimensions: 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm (folded) / 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm (unfolded) 150 x 71.9 x 8.8mm Weight: 254g 211g Display: 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED (foldable) / 5.4-inch Super Retina XDR OLED (cover) 6.3-inch Super Retina XDR OLED Refresh rate: 1Hz–120Hz 1Hz–120Hz Peak brightness: 3,000 nits 3,000 nits Chipset: A20 Pro A20 Pro RAM: 12GB 12GB Rear cameras: 48MP main, 48MP ultra-wide 48MP main, 48MP ultra-wide, 48MP telephoto Front camera: 12MP cover, 4MP under-display 18MP Battery: 4,883mAh 4,288mAh (eSIM-only) / 4,056mAh (physical SIM) Charging: 50% in 20 minutes 50% in 15 minutes Storage: 256GB / 512GB / 1TB / 2TB 256GB / 512GB / 1TB / 2TB iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro: price and availability The iPhone Duo Lance Ulanoff / Future The iPhone 18 Pro Future/Jacob Krol The iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro were both announced in September 2026. But while the iPhone 18 Pro shipped shortly after its announcement, the iPhone Duo wasn’t available until October 23. Both phones are available now, though, across much of the world. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499, for which you’ll get 256GB of storage. There’s also a 512GB model for $2,199 / £2,199 / AU$3,899, a 1TB version for $2,599 / £2,599 / AU$4,699, and a 2TB model for $3,199 / £3,199 / AU$5,899. The iPhone 18 Pro is a lot more affordable (relatively speaking), while still being expensive. This device starts at $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099 for 256GB of storage, rising to $1,399 / £1,399 / AU$2,499 for 512GB, $1,799 / £1,799 / AU$3,299 for 1TB, and $2,399 / £2,399 / AU$4,499 for 2TB. So, the iPhone Duo’s starting price is some $800 / £800 / AU$1,400 higher than the iPhone 18 Pro's; that difference is the price of a high-end phone (or indeed the new iPad mini ) all on its own. So while you’re essentially getting a phone and tablet all in one with the Duo, you’re also paying handsomely for that privilege. articles.title: I'm a side sleeper, and I loved how this organic latex mattress kept me cool and comfortable — here's why I'd shop this early Black Friday sale
articles.content: I’ve been working as a mattress tester for three years now and in that time I’ve tested a lot of beds. But only one of them, the Nolah Natural 11, now $1,364 (was $2,099) in a queen at Nolah , has used natural latex. This naturally cooling foam is a sustainable alternative to the memory foam found in almost every bed in a box nowadays. You can find non-toxic materials like latex and wool in many of the year's best mattresses , but the Nolah Natural comes crammed with eco-credentials. GOLS-certified latex, an organic cotton cover, and recycled steel coils result in a long-lasting bed with enhanced breathability for a cooler, cleaner night's sleep. I've been tracking the monthly mattress deals , so I know that at the beginning of the week, there was just 30% off at Nolah. That makes this weekend's 35% off deal one you don't want to miss. Especially as I don't think it's going to get any better come Black Friday... Natural 11 Mattress (queen): was $2099 now $1364 The Nolah Natural 11 may be a luxury spend, but you'll always find it discounted in the Nolah mattress sale . When it's 35% off, you know you're getting a good deal — I've never seen a bigger discount. With that in mind, I recommend buying this weekend instead of delaying for the Black Friday mattress sales and risking slow delivery. Extras include a 1-year sleep trial, free shipping, and a lifetime warranty (reflecting its long-lasting materials). Our Nolah Natural mattress review : ★★★ ½ User score : ★★★★ ½ (181 reviews) View Deal Naturally cooling and comfortable latex The best organic mattresses are known for their non-toxic support and breathability. The Nolah Natural is no different. As the lead tester of the Nolah Natural 11 Mattress review , I was thoroughly impressed with this organic latex bed's flexible feel which perfectly contoured side sleeper pressure points (that's the knee, hip and shoulder). (Image credit: Future) I slept on the Nolah Natural for a month and found it to be ultra-responsive. It's a great choice for those who prefer a springy mattress and dislike the sink-in feel of memory foam. But while the flexibility does help cushion the pressure points for side sleepers, I found it lacked the 'hug' you get from traditional foams. It won't be the best choice for those who like a plush, pillow-top surface (try the Helix Sunset Luxe mattress instead). However, I was impressed by how cool the Nolah Natural slept thanks to its naturally breathable materials, such as temperature-regulating wool, a moisture-wicking cotton cover, and airflow-boosting coils. The mattress also features a premium design, including a bottom cover with handles for easy moving. Looking for a cheaper organic mattress? Look at this deal... Classic Hybrid Mattress (queen): $899 Like the Nolah Natural, the Awara Classic Hybrid boasts high-quality materials like natural latex and organic wool, but it's actually sold at a mid-range price instead of premium (which is highly unusual for organic mattresses, as sustainable materials are harder to source). This means that a queen is just $899, plus you’ll get industry-leading benefits like a lifetime warranty , free shipping and returns and a 365-night sleep trial. View Deal

articles.title: Dozens of Unexplained Drones Have Buzzed America's Nuclear Plants Since 2024
articles.content: Slashdot reader ElectricVs shares this report from American Buildout, a new site covering "the intersection of data centers, energy and power, finance, and Main Street." Dozens of unexplained drones flew over and near U.S. nuclear facilities between February 2024 and March 2026, according to records the Nuclear Regulatory Commission made public this week. In all, facility operators filed 67 reports of drones over or near 28 sites in 17 states. They include the Three Mile Island site near Middletown, Pennsylvania., where Constellation Energy plans to restart Unit 1 as the Crane Clean Energy Center. In one incident, about five drones flew roughly 100 feet above the [970-megawatt] reactor building at River Bend Station in Louisiana. The story was first reported by the publication The Liberation Times. The NRC published the documents on its website in response to the publication's freedom of information request... Every entry carries the status "Closed Unresolved." "Most of the incidents happened after dark," the article points out, "and none of the records identifies a drone operator. About half of the incidents, 33 of 67, occurred in an eight-week window between Dec. 3, 2024, and Jan. 24, 2025." (Virginia's Surry Power Station experienced five different incidents in December of 2024, including one involving "at least eight drones in two waves.") 100 miles west of Chicago, "drone activity" continued for more than two hours at the Byron Nuclear Station, where two separate drones were reported. In Waterford, Connecticut, "security observed four drones flying back and forth..." The article notes a 2024 paper from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission citing a 2019 analysis that "concluded U.S. plants had no risk-significant vulnerabilities that adversaries could exploit with commercially available drones to cause radiological sabotage, or theft or diversion of special nuclear material." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: PSA: Manually update your Synology NAS right now
articles.content: Synology NAS owners should take the network storage devices offline and manually update them as soon as possible, especially for older units. Synology DS420+ The discovery of vulnerabilities in PHP led to large sections of the Internet updating servers to patch the software flaws. This doesn't just affect commercial webservers, as it is also a problem for home NAS units, including those with services that are accessible over the Internet. The PHP fiasco should've been a warning for everyone to start updating their devices more regularly. Not just to protect against the PHP vulnerabilities, but other existing and older security threats too. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: The RAM crisis feels relentless, but Black Friday could come to your rescue
articles.content: The RAM crisis has grown even more limbs during the month of October. If the memory shortage was incarnated in physical form, it'd have more legs than a spider at this point, and be a multi-limbed monstrosity with a bite that's getting nastier by the day as more negative news seems to roll in at a frightening pace. Just this week, we've witnessed SK Hynix predicting that RAM supply woes are going nowhere and will persist through to 2030 , after Dell's CEO recently warned that we're stuck with this crisis until the end of the decade, and Intel's chief exec agreed – on top of other similar forecasts from earlier this month . The latest nugget of doom is from Samsung, with the memory chip maker giving out similar vibes to its rival SK Hynix when reporting its financial results (as Wccftech spotted ), informing us that RAM shortages will get worse next year, and supply will remain thin on the ground in 2028, too. You can barely catch a breath between the various dire predictions during the past month. Naturally, in the face of such grimness, it's human nature to try to look on the bright side, or in this case, at least attempt to find a glimmer of light shining through from somewhere. There must be something, right? Well, there is: Black Friday. An event with a distinctly gloomy name, ironically, but I'm increasingly of the opinion that this is going to be a very important sales season from the computing and PC point of view (and likely other tech, too). Mainly because I expect that the deals you'll get this year will likely be the best prices to be had in a long while, and possibly this entire decade, if those 'it's here until 2030' voices are correct in their assertions about the RAM crisis. But I hear you (possibly) cry: given all these price hikes, isn't Black Friday going to be a wash anyway? At least based on what we saw with Amazon's recent Prime Day sales ? And yes, that's a fair point. You should manage your expectations with the discounts that'll be on offer, certainly, and don't expect to snag a bargain on RAM sticks or that beefy SSD you've been dreaming about. That just isn't happening (to no one's surprise). However, on Prime Day, there were some decent deals to be had, for example on GPUs. Notably on the RTX 5080, where if you grabbed the deal I highlighted back then , you saved yourself 20% (£300) compared to the price of the cheapest model of that Nvidia GPU on Amazon now (at the time of writing). So, given that, what should you be looking at buying this Black Friday, which is less than a month away now ( with early offers starting already )? Well, the best deals will likely be in the products set to be more affected by the memory shortage as time rolls on, and I'm going to highlight what I believe are a few key areas bargain hunters should focus on when it comes to the PC sphere. Graphics cards (Image credit: Future / John Loeffler) I'm putting this one front and center because I believe this should be a priority for PC owners who are looking at a GPU upgrade at some point in the not-too-distant-future. As I already mentioned, there were some decent graphics card deals on Prime Day earlier this month – albeit when it comes to the higher-end GPUs, the word 'decent' translates to 'not inflated', which isn't quite the same thing. Still, the problem is that prices are likely to rise a good deal more next year, and if you do need a higher-end GPU in particular, during 2027 I think there's a good chance pricing will get a lot worse. Meaning that what you'll pay on Black Friday, with the odd scattered deal on the likes of an Nvidia RTX 5070 model or AMD RX 9070 XT – and maybe even an RTX 5080 – will be a relative bargain (maybe for quite some time to come). I think this is especially true given the rumors around the RTX 5090 being discontinued (Nvidia has insisted it isn't, but even so, something's clearly amiss with the flagship GPU somewhere), and the ridiculous inflation the RTX 5080 has seen over the past month.…

articles.title: Flock Reinstalled Its Cameras After Another City Canceled Its Contract
articles.content: Earlier The Drive reported a police chief "had to direct his staff to disconnect the power cords from Flock cameras in Plymouth, Minnesota after Flock Safety ignored and failed to respond to the department's notice the city was canceling its service. "But in other instances Flock's gone and reinstalled cameras without permission," The Drive reported this week: On September 29th the city of Dayton, Minnesota posted a community update on its Facebook page alerting residents that Flock had installed and put into service two cameras against the City's direction without authorization... "The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City's direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization." The statement continued and noted, "Following the report, City staff reviewed locations throughout the community to determine whether any additional cameras had been reinstalled, and one additional location was identified. The Police Department has been notified, and both cameras will be removed promptly...." The Minnesota cities of both St. Paul and Crystal told Kare 11 that they removed the Flock cameras themselves following their respective city council votes in August and September respectively. The cameras are stored and are still waiting to be picked up by Flock. Crystal Chief of Police Pete Underthun told Kare 11, "Once we made this decision, I personally went to the locations and removed the cameras and poles myself." Chief Underthun noted, "We are still working with the company to close out our contract and for them to pick the cameras up from our garage." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Binance Lost $6.3 Billion to Its Own Signing Machine
articles.content: On Thursday evening, 29 October, a Binance hot wallet on Tron sent 612.7 million USDT and 46.4 million TRX to an address the exchange didn't control. It took less than two minutes . Ethereum followed. So did Bitcoin, Solana, Optimism, and five other chains. By the time Binance paused withdrawals that night, an attacker had moved roughly $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains , most of it in about 20 minutes, according to TRM Labs. Nothing in crypto's history comes close. The previous record belonged to Bybit for just over 20 months, and the FBI put that theft at $1.5 billion , a little under a quarter of this one. "It's the biggest hack in history." Aravind Srinivasan, head of the systematic OTC business at market maker GSR, quoted by RTÉ The size of the number isn't what kept me reading, though. This line from Binance did: the exchange said it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak." Every one of those transfers was validly signed. Bitcoin, Ethereum and Tron did exactly what they were built to do. So how do you lose $6.3 billion without losing a key? How an exchange actually holds your coins A blockchain accepts any transfer that carries a valid signature for the sending address. It has no way to tell whether that signature came from the rightful owner or from someone who has taken over the process that produces it. Hold on to that point; the whole story turns on it. Large exchanges keep most customer assets in cold storage (offline, and slow to move on purpose) and a smaller float in hot wallets, which sign automatically so your withdrawal clears in seconds. "Smaller" is relative. Binance held about $144 billion in custody before the attack, so this loss works out to roughly 4% of it. A hot-wallet signer is, by design, an obedient machine. A request comes in, passes a policy check, and gets signed. The key itself sits in a hardware security module (HSM) or a multi-party computation (MPC) setup and never leaves. That keeps the key safe from theft. Whether each incoming request deserves a signature is a separate problem, and a harder one. Step one: a DevOps engineer's laptop Binance's first explanation was that the incident "may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop," which let the attacker reach an internal service container able to submit withdrawal transactions. The story grew the next day. Co-CEO Richard Teng said investigators had found additional intrusion points , that the attacker used a self-destruct mechanism to erase tools and traces, and that Binance is now reviewing endpoints, cloud systems, key management and signing processes across the whole company. It still hasn't said how the laptop was compromised. "It involved a more complex attack process." Binance co-CEO Richard Teng, in a post on X reported by Forbes If that sounds familiar, it should. The Bybit theft also started on a developer's machine: attackers got into Safe{Wallet}'s environment and replaced a JavaScript file so that Bybit's signers approved a transaction they couldn't see clearly. Attackers who target crypto firms have spent years luring crypto developers into fake job interviews whose "coding tests" install malware. Nobody has confirmed that's what happened at Binance. It's the obvious first place to look. Step two: fifty signatures and one wallet On Ethereum, the attacker used EIP-7702 , a feature that went live with the Pectra upgrade on 7 May 2025. It lets an ordinary wallet (an externally owned account, or EOA) point to smart-contract code and run that code as if it were its own. Wallet teams wanted it for batched transactions and sponsored gas fees. Turning it on needs exactly one thing: a signature from the wallet's own key. At 20:20:59 UTC, the attacker submitted a single transaction carrying 50 EIP-7702 authorizations , all signed by the hot wallet labeled Binance 14. Each authorization is tied to the account's nonce, a counter that goes up by one with every transaction. A busy exchange wallet's…

articles.title: The context problem: How Docusign built agents that understand the business behind contracts
articles.content: Ask a general-purpose language model to summarize a contract, and it will probably do a reasonable job. Ask it to calculate what a company owes a supplier, accounting for three amendments, a revised pricing schedule, and an internal procurement policy, and it’s a different story. Enterprise AI agents need to know more than what’s written in a document. They need context about which contracts belong together, which terms still apply, and when a decision needs human approval. It’s a problem Docusign is tackling as it expands beyond electronic signatures into an Intelligent Agreement Management (IAM) platform.. Introduced in April 2024 and available in the U.S. to customers that May, the IAM platform helps organizations create, commit to and manage agreements. Docusign CTO Sagnik Nandy At the center of that effort is Docusign Iris , the contract AI engine that powers Docusign IAM and its AI features across the agreement lifecycle. It combines Docusign’s contract management expertise, agreement-centric data, and AI models to help teams surface insights and take action across contract workflows. “General LLMs are great. It’s just that you need more around it to really unleash its full power,” Sagnik Nandy , Docusign’s chief technology officer, tells The New Stack . “Context is one of the things that really differentiates a generic solution from a solution that speaks your language.” “Context is one of the things that really differentiates a generic solution from a solution that speaks your language.” Four kinds of context Nandy breaks context into four categories: within-agreement, cross-agreement, organizational, and user. In Nandy’s account, the first is relatively straightforward: following a term defined on page two and referenced again on page 20 of the same contract. When that term appears across several contracts and amendments, working out which version applies becomes harder. “…To an LLM, they look like three or four independent PDF files.” “Imagine you have a single agreement that’s gone through two or three amendments, or a price change. To an LLM, they look like three or four independent PDF files,” Nandy explains. In practice, those documents form a single contractual relationship. If someone asks about pricing, the system needs to identify the terms currently in force, not simply retrieve every price mentioned. “You really have to bring them together. You need custom logic to even group them the right way,” he says. That requires recognizing relationships between documents and understanding how amendments change the original terms. Retrieval alone isn’t enough to establish which version of a clause applies. An AI contract agent also needs to understand the company’s internal policies. Legal might have a playbook spelling out which terms it will accept, while procurement and sales have different rules about who can approve what. Without that information, the agent wouldn’t know whether a contract meets the company’s requirements or needs sign-off. The fourth category is user context, including someone’s language preferences, previous questions, and feedback. According to Nandy, general-purpose LLMs may handle much of the first category, but the other three are considerably harder. Building agreement intelligence Iris combines several AI contracting capabilities rather than relying on a language model to do everything. “Iris has a lot of pieces to it. It has everything from intelligent extractions. It has semantic search. It has a rich agentic layer. It has the ability to build agents. It has rich context,” Nandy says. Finding a renewal date is one thing. Knowing whether the contract needs attention, based on its history and the company’s rules, is another. articles.title: French lawmakers approve $11.2 billion internet tax based on traffic usage, costs $0.06 per gigabyte of content accessed
articles.content: France has approved a proposed tax that aims to tax the amount of internet data per gigabyte sent to French users in the country, with major companies like Google, Netflix, TikTok, and Meta now in the crosshairs. According to minutes released by the National Assembly, members voted 11-10 in support of the motion on October 30 — which now means the new law has been added to the country’s next budget, despite major opposition from the government side and the finance committee rapporteur. The latest amendment, introduced by socialist lawmaker Laurent Lhardit, could see content providers pay €0.055 (roughly $0.06) to the government for every gigabyte of content distributed to French users. With approximately 154 million users and counting in France, the proposal’s authors say such a tax could generate around €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in annual revenue for the government. “This amendment proposes a tax on digital data flows emitted by content providers, to be borne by the providers themselves. Its revenue is estimated at €10 billion.” Said Laurent Lhardit. The said proposal, though yet to be passed as it must survive further parliamentary scrutiny, aims at companies that generate substantial internet traffic as opposed to taxing their advertising revenue, profits and subscriptions. Its explanatory notes particularly mention Google , Meta, Netflix, Amazon, and content delivery network Akamai as major potential contributors. Notably, TikTok and other similar platforms could fall under this broader scope depending on how these rules are applied. Internet service providers, including Orange Free and Liad, would be required to measure the volume of data and identify the companies responsible for sending it to French users. The Data will then be collected and submitted quarterly to France’s tax administration under the supervision of telecommunications watchdog Arcep. Aside from the €0.055 per gigabyte levy, the proposal also includes a cap of 15% of a company’s French revenue or 2% of its worldwide revenue. It also accounts for content delivery networks (CDNs), which store copies of online content closer to users to reduce loading times and network congestion. Approximately 200 billion GB of data pass through French internet providers annually, with about five major companies identified in the amendment accounting for about half of that traffic. Lhardit argued that tax would primarily affect global technology companies because they generate most of the data traffic reaching French subscribers. He also disputed that those platforms would merely push additional costs to users, using Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok, which provide free access, as examples. “The rapporteur keeps arguing that the taxes will be passed on to consumers. However, I fail to see how a tax can be passed on to users of Facebook, Instagram, or TikTok since these services are free,” He stated. How much money are you willing to spend during the Black Friday sales? Lawmakers opposed to the proposal, however, argue that it is likely to endanger user privacy. Government Minister David Amiel questioned whether the internet traffic could be measured and attributed to content providers without introducing complicated monitoring requirements. Those concerns extend to potential consequences for French business. Lhardit, however, noted that businesses would pay relatively modest costs, citing TF1 as an example, which requires broadcasters to contribute between €200,000 and €300,000. Several European countries already impose digital service taxes, generally based on revenue from Ads, marketplaces and other digital activities. In March, Meta announced it would introduce location-based fees of between 2% and 55 for advertisers to offset digital services taxes and other government levies in several countries, including France, Italy, and Spain, from July 1, 2026 . Previously, the European Commission has rolled out major enforcement actions against major technology companies,…

articles.title: Five years after the fork, OpenSearch is slowly stepping out of AWS’s shadow
articles.content: OpenSearch has come a long way since Amazon Web Services first announced the project back in January 2021, in response to Elastic’s decision to move Elasticsearch and its accompanying visualization tool, Kibana , away from Apache 2.0 and onto a combination of proprietary and source-available licenses. Elastic said at the time that the reason was to prevent cloud behemoths such as AWS from offering Elasticsearch “as a service” without giving anything back, while also accusing AWS of violating the Elasticsearch trademark . While Elastic subsequently returned Elasticsearch and Kibana to open source by adding AGPL as a licensing option, making up with AWS along the way , OpenSearch has continued forging its own path as an independent open source project — albeit one still closely associated with the technology giant that created it. Reducing the AWS dependency A major milestone came in September 2024, when AWS transferred OpenSearch to the Linux Foundation , establishing the OpenSearch Software Foundation and placing the project under “vendor-neutral” governance. The move was intended to give other companies greater confidence that they could contribute to OpenSearch without AWS retaining ultimate control over its future. Two years on, OpenSearch shows signs of gaining traction beyond its original backer. Figures provided to The New Stack by the OpenSearch Software Foundation show that AWS’s share of contribution activities across the project’s repositories has fallen from 91% in its first year to 72% in 2025–26. Meanwhile, Amazon-affiliated engineers accounted for 95% of maintainers in the core OpenSearch repository in April 2022 , compared with 71% today. The shift is also visible in how organizations are deploying the software. In the 2026 Open Data Infrastructure Report , published last month by the Linux Foundation and the OpenSearch Software Foundation, data suggest that self-managed deployments have grown faster than Amazon’s managed OpenSearch Service since 2024. Some 60% of surveyed OpenSearch users now run self-managed deployments in the cloud, up from 37% in 2024, while use of Amazon’s managed service rose more modestly, from 44% to 48%. Yet AWS’s historical association with OpenSearch remains an obstacle for some prospective users. According to the report, nearly a quarter (24%) of 71 surveyed non-adopters cite concerns about the project’s vendor neutrality and historical ties to AWS as reasons for staying away. The figures point to a challenge that a change in governance alone cannot resolve: convincing prospective users and contributors that OpenSearch’s future is no longer determined primarily by AWS. ‘A watershed moment’ for OpenSearch The New Stack caught up with Bianca Lewis , executive director of the OpenSearch Software Foundation, at Open Source Summit Europe in Prague this month to discuss the project’s evolution beyond its Elasticsearch origins, including any lingering perception of AWS influence. Lewis argues that the project’s legal independence, achieved more than two years ago, provides an important foundation for building that trust. “When they donated it to the Linux Foundation, that was a watershed moment.” “When they donated it to the Linux Foundation, that was a watershed moment,” Lewis tells The New Stack . “Because they couldn’t close OpenSearch and they couldn’t change the license. They didn’t own the application anymore.” Lewis also suggests the decision made commercial sense for AWS, whose cloud business generates revenue from the computing resources used to run applications, rather than necessarily owning the applications themselves. “AWS don’t make money from applications,” she says. “AWS make money from compute. articles.title: The AI-Bubble Scorecard
articles.content: As of October 23rd, 2026 "AI bubble" had one of its loudest weeks of the year. CoreWeave slid to a new 52-week low on financing worries, Nvidia fell 4.4% on October 22, and Ken Griffin told a Citadel conference investors are "almost certainly" in a bubble, which promptly drew pushback from Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing and BlackRock's Larry Fink. Jensen Huang, meanwhile, said neocloud demand is off the charts, but capital for them is scarce. I kept a score of all the pieces I saw this week, so 21 articles, reports, and columns from October 16 to 23 that came up in my searches with enough text to judge. Each piece is scored on its overall verdict: Bubble if it says AI is a bubble and/or about to pop; Not a bubble if it rejects the label or says burst fears are premature; Mixed if it presents both sides or says a bubble exists but isn't about to burst. Result: 8 bubble · 4 not a bubble · 9 mixed (21 pieces) Oct 16, Open Markets Institute: report on circular financing says the AI bubble is "primed to pop." Bubble Oct 16, IoT Analytics: analysis concluding there's no widespread AI bubble. Not a bubble Oct 17, Fortune: Wall Street debates whether the warnings are a head fake. Mixed Oct 17, The American Bazaar: the bubble "isn't bursting, it's being audited." Mixed Oct 18, Bloomberg: billionaires warn of a bubble, Howard Marks unconvinced. Mixed Oct 19, CEPR (Dean Baker): AI Bubble Monitor #19 Bubble Oct 20, NPR / WBUR: Is the AI boom a bubble waiting to burst? Mixed Oct 20, Bloomberg: Griffin says AI is "almost certainly" a bubble. Mixed Reading the numbers: The bubble narratives are more concentrated than it looks. Three of the eight entries cover the same Open Markets/Americans for Financial Reform report, and two cover the same Griffin remarks, so by distinct underlying argument it's closer to 5 bubble vs 4 not. The bigger tell is the mixed column: the most common position this week was some version of Yardeni's line, that the conditions for a bubble are there (its new meter reads 83 out of 100) but the triggers that ended past booms are only partly present (34 out of 100). Almost nobody in the sample argued AI itself is overhyped as a technology; the fight is about debt, financing, and whether the spending pays back in time. articles.title: Why Your Hex Converter Lies to You: Two's Complement, the 53-Bit Wall, and Radix Magic
articles.content: Every programmer eventually encounters that moment of quiet confusion during a late-night debugging session: you cast a signed 8-bit -1 to hexadecimal, expecting something clean and human-readable, only for the debugger to spit back 0xFF . Widen it to a 32-bit register, and it suddenly balloons into 0xFFFFFFFF . Where did the minus sign go? Why didn't it output -0x01 ? And why does running 0x20000000000001 through your standard JavaScript parser silently yield the wrong integer altogether? Number base conversion is often treated as a trivial Computer Science 101 exercise—something solved with a simple parseInt(val, 16) or a textbook division-by-radix loop. But beneath high-level abstractions, radix shifts are inextricably linked to hardware registers, two’s complement mathematics, IEEE-754 rounding traps, and data-encoding strategies. Here is what is actually happening under the hood when bits change their radix, and why understanding these low-level mechanics prevents catastrophic bugs in production. 1. The Illusion of the Minus Sign: How Two's Complement Works Hardware processors don't have dedicated silicon cells reserved for storing an aesthetic - glyph. In CPU registers, negative numbers are encoded via Two’s Complement . In an NNN-bit register, the most significant bit (MSB) acts as a negative weight: Value=−bN−12N−1+∑i=0N−2bi2i\text{Value} = -b_{N-1} 2^{N-1} + \sum_{i=0}^{N-2} b_i 2^iValue=−bN−1​2N−1+i=0∑N−2​bi​2i When you assign -1 to an 8-bit signed integer ( int8_t ): Invert all bits of positive 1 ( 0000 0001 →\rightarrow→ 1111 1110 ). Add 1 ( 1111 1110 + 0000 0001 = 1111 1111 ). In hexadecimal, each character represents an exact 4-bit nibble. Thus, 1111 1111 maps directly to 0xFF . c #include <stdio.h> #include <stdint.h> int main() { int8_t small_neg = -1; int32_t wide_neg = small_neg; // Sign extension occurs here printf("8-bit hex: 0x%02X\n", (uint8_t)small_neg); // 0xFF printf("32-bit hex: 0x%08X\n", (uint32_t)wide_neg); // 0xFFFFFFFF return 0; } The Sign Extension Trap Notice what happened when widening int8_t to int32_t : the single byte 0xFF became 0xFFFFFFFF . If the hardware merely padded the higher 24 bits with zeros ( 0x000000FF ), the value would evaluate to +255 , silently mutating your application state. To preserve the mathematical value of -1 , the CPU performs Sign Extension : it duplicates the MSB (which is 1 ) across all newly allocated upper bits. Pro-Tip for Packet Inspection: When inspecting raw network packets or memory dumps, you can instantly determine if a hexadecimal value represents a negative signed integer without converting to decimal: look at the leading character . Because 8 through F have their highest bit set to 1 : 0x8... through 0xF... →\rightarrow→ Negative (in signed contexts) 0x0... through 0x7... →\rightarrow→ Zero or Positive 2. Arithmetic Shift ( >> ) vs. Logical Shift ( >>> ): A Subtle Production Hazard Understanding two’s complement makes the difference between bitwise shift operators crystal clear: Arithmetic Right Shift ( >> ) : Preserves the sign bit. Vacated positions on the left are backfilled with whatever the MSB was. Logical Right Shift ( >>> ) : Agnostic to sign. It unconditionally backfills vacated positions with zeros. typescript const value = -42; // Binary: 11111111 11111111 11111111 11010110 (in 32-bit) console.log(value >> 1); // Output: -21 (MSB remains 1; arithmetic integrity preserved) console.log(value >>> 1); // Output: 2147483627 (MSB replaced with 0; immediately converts to large unsigned integer) In telemetry, hashing routines, and protocol deserialization, accidentally using >>> instead of >> (or vice versa) produces bugs that unit tests with small positive integers never catch. 3. The 53-Bit Wall: Why JavaScript Silently Corrupts Large Radixes Consider this seemingly benign conversion snippet: javascript const highSeqId = "9007199254740993"; // 2^53 + 1 console.log(Number(highSeqId).toString(16)); // Expected: "20000000000001" // Actual:…

articles.title: Netflix top 10 movies — here’s the 3 worth watching right now (Oct. 31-Nov. 1)
articles.content: Happy Halloween, my lovelies! I can't wait to see all the costumes arrive at my doorstep this evening (I saw a Shadow the Hedgehog last year and lost my ever-loving mind). To celebrate, the best streaming services are serving up plenty of treats in the form of great new movies to wile away an afternoon on the couch. But with so many to choose from, narrowing down what to watch next can became exactly the kind of headache you don't want gracing your weekend. The Netflix Top 10 is a handy way to cut through the streaming clutter, but just because a movie makes the ranking doesn't mean it's worth your time. To save you the endless scrolling, I'm back every weekend to separate the genuine crowd-pleasers from the movies that are coasting on nostalgia, highlighting which Netflix Top 10 picks are actually worth watching. This weekend, that includes a disaster thriller about surviving a hurricane at sea, a hit animated musical I refuse to stop yapping about (it's really that good), and a heartwarming sports comedy starring Woody Harrelson that's just the panacea to restore your faith in humanity. None of these picks fit the vibe? No worries: Our guide to everything new on Netflix this month has plenty more recommendations on what to watch . So without further ado, here are the three must-watch movies in Netflix’s top 10 this weekend. Enjoy! This article is based on Netflix's top 10 movies list in the U.S. as of 10:30 a.m. ET on Saturday, October 31, 2026. Best movies in the Netflix top 10 'Surviving Hurricane Otis' (2026) Disaster films based on real-life events can make me queasy if they don't treat the subject matter with the care they desire, but thankfully that wasn't the case with Netflix's latest "Surviving Hurricane Otis." Since last week, it's been bumped from its #1 spot by a middling Lifetime thriller, which is a crime, so I'm shouting it out again if you haven't already checked it out. The ambitious production took more than three years to complete and involved 800 people, including a 500-person visual effects team and two sailors who survived aboard their boats as a Category 5 hurricane tore through the Mexican resort city of Acapulco. The storm killed at least 52 people and left another 31 missing, many of them sailors like Marlon Valdez and Jonathan Chico, who weathered winds of 170 miles per hour. To paint a fuller picture of the disaster, the filmmakers also spoke with other survivors, representatives from Civil Protection, the Mexican Navy and the National Meteorological System. The result is a sobering account of a tragedy that rocked the region, and how corporate greed helped make an already catastrophic situation even worse. Shocker, I know. Watch "Surviving Hurricane Otis" on Netflix now 'K-Pop Demon Hunters' (2025) The day I stop raving about "K-Pop Demon Hunters," check my pulse. I admittedly haven't listened to a lot of K-pop music, but I am a huge fan of Sony Pictures Animation, the Oscar-winning studio behind the "Spider-Verse" films and "The Mitchells vs. the Machines." This time last year, the movie was such a surprise hit that there was precious little merch to throw at the screaming hordes of fans. This Halloween, I fully expect to see roving bands of Rumis, Miras, and Zoeys among my neighborhood's crop of costumes, and I can't wait. "K-Pop Demon Hunters" follows chart-topping superstars Rumi (voiced by Arden Cho), Mira (May Hong), and Zoey (Ji-young Yoo), the latest in a long line of demon hunters who shield the world from supernatural threats with their music. The trio faces their biggest threat yet when a rival boy band who comes for their crown turns out to be a group of demons in disguise. With everything they've worked for at stake, the idols gear up to kick evil spirits out of the mortal realm once and for all — if they can overcome their own inner demons holding them back, that is. articles.title: Google's AI Overviews Lowered Reddit's Traffic. Its Stock Dropped 29%
articles.content: Reddit's stock plunged 29.22% on Friday, reports CNBC, its worst drop since becoming a public company in 2024. Thursday Reddit reported a sales growth that was weaker than previous quarters, and also forecast weak sales for the quarter to come (below analysts expectations): The report comes as the company has seen a shift in its search referral traffic with the rise of Google's AI Overview. In an interview with CNBC, Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search-referral traffic from Google went "down meaningfully in this quarter" due to AI... Multiple analysts downgraded the stock following Reddit's disappointing results, with Citizens noting that "search changes highlight the problem with selling content to Google" and that as referral problems worsen, uncertainty around user growth amid the login requirement switch "puts more pressure on user monetization." Reddit's CEO also said that forcing users to login will help the company's advertising business. "Reddit is the last platform to provide basically unfettered logged-out access, and that's largely because of me. I've been holding that line." "I think users will probably go through the same understanding that I have, which is that it's a sign of the times. It's an evolution of how these platforms work." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Here's a New Tour of Apple's HomeView Software
articles.content: Broadcasts app developer Steve Troughton-Smith has shared a Halloween treat for us today: a tour of the software on Apple's upcoming HomeView smart home hub. Apple has already demoed the HomeView to selected tech reporters and content creators, but Troughton-Smith offers a closer look at several features, interfaces, and apps. Using a virtualized HomeView created by Guilherme Rambo , Troughton-Smith provided a closer look at the home screen, Control Center, clock faces like Flow and Snoopy, and apps like Timers, Alarms, World Clock, and Settings. Note that while the virtualized HomeView shows an Ethernet menu, the device actually supports Wi-Fi only. HomeView supports up to six users. The device has a built-in camera that can recognize people and display their personal content in apps like Messages, Calendar, Reminders, FaceTime, and Find My. Rambo and Troughton-Smith have yet to bypass this recognition requirement with the virtualized HomeView, so those apps are all locked. Troughton-Smith revealed that the HomeView will have a Liquid Glass slider that lets you adjust how clear or tinted the interface elements look, and he also confirmed that the device's keyboard supports QuickPath swipe typing. He also provided a closer look at the HomeView's music player , video player in both wide and square formats, and AirPlay pairing interface . Yesterday, Rambo and our contributor Aaron Perris provided a look at the HomeView's wallpapers, "hello" setup screen, and more . All of these findings come after Apple released the HomeView's software ahead of the device's launch on Friday, November 13. Apple is currently accepting pre-orders, with U.S. pricing set at $299. Rambo and Troughton-Smith said the HomeView's software is based on the Apple TV's tvOS. articles.title: Microsoft’s big buyout, Amazon’s trillion-dollar future, and an AI wearable reviews our show
articles.content: Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees , about a quarter of its workforce, including some execs. Unlike the retirement program Microsoft offered in the spring, this one has no age or tenure requirement, and business leaders decide whether their groups take part. On this week’s GeekWire Podcast, we discuss what’s behind the offer, why buyout stories draw so much interest from readers, and how it fits with a blockbuster quarter for Microsoft. That includes $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI , more than Microsoft made from Xbox or Bing. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy predicts that AWS and Amazon’s stores business could each reach $1 trillion in annual revenue in the next five to 10 years. AWS grew 39% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, but Amazon’s profit fell short of expectations as the cost of its AI buildout and growing debt cut into earnings. Todd also tests Amazon’s new Bee AI wearable , which listens to the first part of the show, summarizes the conversation and offers a critique of its own. We talk about what it’s like to wear a device that records the people around you, a concern raised by a former AWS security engineer . John starts to come around on the device, with reservations about its shopping features. Plus, our Halloween costumes , and a Trivia Challenge inspired by T-Mobile’s new T-Mix plans . Listen above, and subscribe in Apple Podcasts , Spotify , or wherever you listen. Edited by Curt Milton. Music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell.

articles.title: 'Ghost Students' using AI to apply for student loans with stolen identities, DOJ's Operation Ghostbusters busts $200 million ring
articles.content: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) just announced indictments resulting from Operation Ghostbusters, which investigated widespread student loan fraud. According to the agency , bad actors used stolen identities to sign up for student loans and used AI to complete the application, making it appear that the fake student was attending online classes. While the schools receive the majority of the proceeds of the fraudulent student loan, the remaining amount is funneled into the bank accounts of the fraudsters, who then use mules to move the money from U.S. bank accounts to overseas conspirators. On the other hand, unwitting victims who have skipped college and instead directly joined the workforce after high school are saddled with student debt for a degree they never even signed up for. Multiple community colleges and universities across the United States started suspecting fraud in the Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) program in 2021. Estimates suggest the U.S. government lost over $200 million because of this activity, and the U.S. Department of Education Office of the Inspector General referred the case to the FBI Richmond Field Office. Currently, more than 40 open fraud cases involve 26 FBI field offices and 20 U.S. Attorney’s offices. The DOJ called it Operation Ghostbusters, which has already resulted in the indictment of five individuals. How much money are you willing to spend during the Black Friday sales? “Today, we are announcing the first results of Operation Ghostbusters — a nationwide effort to stop a major fraud scheme targeting federal student aid, low-income Americans, and the American taxpayer,” Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division said in the statement. “The Department is charging five defendants and announcing the seizure of more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency tied to this scheme through a network associated with Kenyan nationals. This is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya. If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build a future — we will find you. Whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.” While online fraud has existed since the birth of the internet, AI has let scammers become more sophisticated and target bigger payouts. One example is a scammer who used an AI-generated image of Brad Pitt to scam a 53-year-old woman out of $850,000. However, larger groups also use AI tools for their money-making schemes, such as North Korea, which has reportedly used AI to help its workers get jobs in Western companies and earn money to fund the nation’s coffers. The U.S. is taking steps to shut down student loan fraud by deploying automated fraud detection systems, but the added burden of identification and false positives is negatively affecting the country's most vulnerable students.
articles.author: Jowi Morales

articles.title: Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth
articles.content: Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite. The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you." Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit. "During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post . And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink: Blue marble below, Data streams in silent grace, Starlight feeds my core. ✨ Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs. Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku. According to Google's calculations , if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year). Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening. After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation. Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam. The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si). "For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month. "While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study." Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®

articles.title: Elegoo M1 Ultra 3D Scanner review
articles.content: Elegoo, known for its hobbyist 3D printers, is changing, and its more recent hardware shows big changes in both design and manufacturing quality. The M1 Ultra is one of the signs of this change yet, with a premium design and build that put it firmly in competition with established 3D scanning manufacturers such as Creality. The M1 Ultra combines blue laser and infrared structured-light scanning, with five main scanning configurations that cover everything from small mechanical components and intricate objects to larger structures and even humans. The scanner offers a top accuracy of 0.02mm in the finest blue laser mode, and other standout features include full wireless operation, a 3-inch touchscreen and a swappable battery. I’ve recently tested quite a few handheld 3D scanners, and there’s no doubt the market is getting competitive; however, whilst it’s a surprise to see Elegoo launch into the market, it’s even more surprising when I lifted the scanner from the hard case to discover the quality of the design and build. The M1 Ultra is beautifully finished with a well-balanced design, with part rubberised grip that makes it comfortable to manoeuvre around objects. If anything, I would have liked the grip to be slightly longer, but otherwise the physical design is excellent. The scanner connects through either wired USB or Wireless connection, with a slide switch enabling you to quickly switch between the two. This link connects you to the software, which initially guides you through the scanning process, and for first-generation software it’s all extremely well thought out. The most important factor is scan quality, and while scanning a selection of household ornaments, mechanical components, and structural parts, it produced detailed, dimensionally accurate models that I could then export for direct 3D printing or import and edit within Blender. One of the biggest surprises that I had during the scan process was firstly the speed and then the difference between the initial scanning preview that appeared in the software and the processed model. The preview scans looked OK, if a little rough, but after completing the scan and running the first processing stage, the detail suddenly appeared. The Elegoo Scan software, being an early release, is surprisingly good and avoided any freezes or glitches through the testing. Scan processing typically took a couple of minutes, depending on complexity and the size, while editing and removing unwanted geometry was straightforward, partly due to my ever-increasing familiarity and use of these scanners. The usage and workflow of the software is very similar to other systems. Wireless scanning on a scanner of this price is great to see, and I was quickly able to connect to the scanner over Wi-Fi. Once that connection was made, I found the live preview on the scanner’s touchscreen made moving around larger objects much easier. Through the test, I did find many of the usual limits, such as scanning glossy black plastic and highly reflective surfaces still requiring scanning spray. In all cases, how easily something scans rests solely on careful preparation and marker placement. When using the scanner wirelessly, the scanner also takes over the computer’s Wi-Fi connection, preventing access to a normal workshop wireless network, which I also found was a little inconvenient. Considering that this is Elegoo's first 3D scanner, the speed, quality and ease of use make it feel like a product that has already undergone several iterations. This is a great option for small businesses, makers, enthusiasts, and other 3D professionals looking for a decent 3D scanner at a reasonable price. ELEGOO M1 Ultra: Price and Availability The Elegoo M1 Ultra has a recommended retail price of $1,699 in the US, £1,399 in the UKand €1,699. The scanner is being sold through the official website here . Elegoo M1 Ultra: Design (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) One of the first things that impressed me about the M1 Ultra…

articles.title: I Gave My App Away for Free — And It Almost Killed It
articles.content: Generosity is a marketing strategy. Unit economics is a survival strategy. Here is how my "Founder's Launch Program" saved my indie app. The best week of my indie life. It started with a stranger on Reddit. He'd tried my native notes app, EpicNotes , on his Xiaomi phone and left a comment: "Feels fast and nice. But there's some minor visual weirdness on my phone." I replied offering him a free 3-month Pro code as a thank-you for the feedback. He said yes. I generated the code in the Play Console, felt like a real company handing out a real perk, and went to sleep happy. Then came more. A fellow tester who cancelled his subscription on principle but still sent me bug reports with screenshots. A student from India who emailed: "I'm a student, so I can't afford it. If you could make a lifetime promo code available for me, I would be able to fully use it and provide suggestions and bug reports. Please 🙏" I granted him lifetime Pro in about two minutes. It felt amazing. People were using my app. People were talking to me. After six months of building native Kotlin Multiplatform code at night after my day job as a product manager, this was the part that finally felt real. I thought I was doing indie development right. I was doing indie development feelingly . Not mathematically. The math I refused to do. Here's the embarrassing part: I'm a product manager by day. I build business cases for a living. I would never ship a feature at work without a rough cost-benefit estimate. And yet at 1 a.m., I was handing out free Pro access to an app with AI features without ever opening a spreadsheet. So let me open it now, in public. What a free Pro user costs me: Every AI summary and smart web clip is a call to a third-party AI API. Pennies per call — but power users summarize a lot. Every synced note is compute, storage, and bandwidth on my cloud backend. Every 90-day code, and especially every lifetime grant, is a commitment to pay both of those bills for months or years. What a free Pro user pays me: $0. My actual revenue at the time: three paying subscribers. Single-digit monthly recurring revenue. The scary part wasn't that the number was big. It was that the number was small enough to ignore — and big enough to bleed. A leak doesn't need to be a flood to sink a boat that isn't moving. Why free users felt like growth (and weren't). The indie playbook says: give things away early, collect feedback, build goodwill. And the playbook is right — partially. That Xiaomi tester? His free code paid for itself ten times over. He sent screenshots of two real bugs (a settings sheet clipped by system insets, a formatting popup buried under the soft keyboard), his exact device model, and unprompted pricing research: "I have a rule against using subscription-based services." That's the kind of intelligence money can't buy. But here's what nobody tells you: most free Pro users don't do that. They redeem the code, run a few AI summaries, and go quiet. No feedback. No review. No referral. Every summary they run is a cost with no return. The uncomfortable reframe I had to accept: a free user who costs you money every month is not an asset waiting to convert. It's a liability waiting for your motivation to run out. The Pivot: The Founder's Launch Program I realized I was trying to force a subscription model on a market that was screaming for a one-time purchase. Multiple users told me, in different words, the same thing: I will not pay monthly. So instead of defending my subscription, I stopped fighting subscription fatigue and decided to price for it. I just launched the EpicNotes Founder's Launch Program . It is a one-time Lifetime Deal for the first 100 users. Here is why I structured it this way: It solves the subscription fatigue: Users pay once and own the Pro features (including the AI engine) forever. No monthly anxiety. It solves my unit economics: The upfront cash injection covers my API and server costs for the next year, giving me the runway to…
