articles.title: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
articles.content: We got a chance to touch Apple’s latest MacBook at the “Pro and Tell” event. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page. Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display Where to Buy: $2899 at Best Buy (w/ $100 gift card) My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions. Read our MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display hands-on .
articles.author: Brad Bourque

articles.title: Developers ask AI which tool to use. Here’s how we track the answer.
articles.content: We asked Claude “Which CMS platforms support MCP integration ?” It searched the web and put Webflow in its first group, Headless and SaaS CMS platforms with hosted MCP servers, sixth in the list, with this line: “A hosted server for managing sites through the Data API, covering pages, components, CMS collections and items, assets, forms, and publishing.” Which CMS platforms support MCP integration? We asked Claude the same question four times. That one was the most detailed of the four, so don’t read it as typical. Webflow got its own bullet in three of the four. Two of those answers said the server works with CMS collections and items, and one said only that it covers the Data API and the Designer. In the fourth run we were one name in a shared bullet with no description. Below, we count how often the engines name Webflow. We asked because AI agents are already one of the ways developers look things up: in Stack Overflow’s 2026 developer survey , nearly 70% of respondents said they use an AI agent to help them find answers. We wanted to see what those agents say when the question is which tool to use. AI picks a first answer for a lot of questions Ask Claude what to use for transactional email and Resend comes up first. Ask what to use for product analytics and PostHog comes up first. We don’t have data on how many developers stop at the first name, but we’d rather be in that first answer than not. What should I use for transactional email? What should I use for product analytics? CMS is the category we care about, and “I need to add a CMS to my website” is how we expect the question to sound. We ran it three times. Webflow was recommended once, last in its group. In the other two it was an example of what you might already use, or it wasn’t named. Sanity, Payload, WordPress, and Ghost showed up in all three. Our question is what it takes to be the default in that category, and we start by measuring where we are today. I need to add a CMS to my website. Why we track it We follow one prompt closely, “Which CMS platforms support MCP integration?” Between Sep 25 and Oct 19 it ran 100 times, 25 on each of four engines. Webflow shows up in 49 of those 100 responses, but the spread by engine is wide, from 22 of 25 on Perplexity to 4 of 25 on Claude. “When an engine leaves us out, the developer asking never sees Webflow, and nothing in our site analytics records it because the question was answered before anyone visited a page.” When an engine leaves us out, the developer asking never sees Webflow, and nothing in our site analytics records it because the question was answered before anyone visited a page. We don’t have referral data that connects these answers to signups or revenue, so we aren’t claiming a revenue effect. What we can measure is whether we’re named, how we’re described, and which sources the engine used. How we track it We use Webflow AEO , under Insights > AEO. The Prompts page lists each tracked prompt with its topic, visibility score, citation rate, and the change from last week. Opening a prompt shows how many responses were tracked, citations split between owned and non-owned domains, citation rate by platform, which of our pages were cited, and a response log you can export. Mention rate is how often Webflow shows up across the prompts we track. It counts a mention whether the description is right or wrong, so we also score the responses we review on four things: whether Webflow is named, which tier it’s placed in (official, community, or not listed), whether the description is accurate, and what type of source the engine used. The dashboard’s visibility score reads 47% for the last 30 days. Our 49 of 100 is a count of responses that named Webflow, so the two won’t match exactly. We’re moving from single prompts to clusters of phrasings. Developers don’t type the same…

articles.title: I checked out three major horror titles in time for Halloween — but a popular movie adaptation ended up being the biggest let down
articles.content: If you celebrate Halloween, you'll no doubt be on the lookout for some things to entertain you this weekend. With this in mind, I checked out three of the biggest new horror releases in October to see if they're any good. Scream or Skip Scream or Skip, that is the question. With so much horror out there to watch and play, our senior entertainment writer, Lucy Buglass, is here to help you decide what's worth your time (or worthy of a Scream) and what's not (so you might want to Skip). Her goal is to help you spend less time scrolling and more time enjoying some great TV shows, movies, and games. Read the full series here. There have been some real highs and lows this month, and I found myself especially disappointed by one movie in particular. Thankfully, there's a great TV show and game to keep you occupied, so it's not all bad. So, what do I recommend checking out this spooky weekend? Scroll down to find out. TV — Crystal Lake Where to watch: Peacock (US); Sky (UK); Stan (AU) Lucy's verdict: Scream Crystal Lake is the anticipated Friday the 13th prequel, and it's a great choice if you want a binge-worthy series to watch over the Halloween weekend. With all eight episodes streaming at once, how could you resist? I did have my reservations about this series, but it is an excellent entry into the horror franchise. In my full Crystal Lake review, I noted there's a clear love for the original movies here, and that it expands upon the lore by focusing on Pamela Voorhees, an under-explored character in the Friday the 13th universe. Played excellently by Linda Cardellini, it's very worth your time. Movie — Other Mommy Where to watch: Theaters worldwide Lucy's verdict: Skip As someone who loved the book Incidents Around the House and was genuinely freaked out by it, I was excited to hear it was getting a movie adaptation. I was even more excited to hear that Jessica Chastain would star in a dual role as a woman and an entity that emulates her, known as "Other Mommy". Unfortunately, the movie ended up being a massive letdown. Not only does it suffer from the cliché of tired and overused jump scares, but it also deviates from the book to the point that it loses the psychological dread and tension that had me looking over my shoulder. Other Mommy does very little to stand out from similar supernatural movies like it Game — Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival Where to play: PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC Lucy's verdict: Scream Hellraiser has been everywhere recently, from its haunted house at Universal's Halloween Horror Nights to a new video game. I was very impressed with Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival and would highly recommend it this Halloween weekend. It's clear it's been made by people who have a genuine appreciation for Hellraiser , as the atmosphere and the willingness to stick to canon are excellent. Iconic character Pinhead returns too, and the result is a gripping game with puzzles and heart-pounding moments.

articles.title: Two US Senators Raise Privacy Concerns About Meta's 'Pervert Glasses'
articles.content: Meta's smart glasses face new questions from two U.S. Senators, reports Gizmodo. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Sen. Edward Markey "are requesting that Meta provide more information before Thanksgiving on whether it conducted detailed human rights due diligence and safety testing on the product before releasing it," reports Gizmodo. The Senators also requested information from Meta about " how it evaluated the privacy risks posed by the glasses, and what kinds of safeguards are currently in place." "Although Meta identified risks to bystander privacy and vulnerable populations before launching its glasses in 2021, it nevertheless launched a product tailor-made for invading the privacy of its users and bystanders," [the senators wrote in a letter Thursday...] The glasses have also been spotted on ICE agents during raids, and have raised potential surveillance concerns. The surveillance fears were even reportedly raised by the New York Police Department's counterterrorism unit in a memo issued earlier this year.... "Meta's own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses' visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers," the senators' letter states, calling the practice an invasion of privacy. "Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people's highly sensitive information for Meta's commercial benefit." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Amazon CEO predicts 6 to 8 AI models will be ‘good enough’ for almost everything
articles.content: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy expects the frontier AI model race to produce several competitive models rather than a single winner, telling analysts on Amazon’s Q3 2026 earnings call Thursday that the challenge ahead will be choosing among models rather than committing to one. “6- 8 models that are about as good as each other, or at least good enough for 95%+ of the workloads.” During the call , Jassy responds to a question from Goldman Sachs analyst Eric Sheridan about the market opportunity for Amazon Bedrock , predicting that within two to three years there will be “6- 8 models that are about as good as each other, or at least good enough for 95%+ of the workloads.” No single AI winner Jassy has seen plenty of technology leaders lose their early advantage over the past 20 years. He pointed to databases and analytics as examples, along with TensorFlow, which once seemed likely to become the standard framework before PyTorch took the lead. He expects something similar to happen with AI models. As Jassy put it, “there is not one tool to rule the world.” Some models will be better at reasoning or coding, while others will have an edge in visual tasks, speed, or cost per token . That leaves companies with plenty of reasons to use more than one. Jassy believes “most customers are going to use multiple models, and many will use multiple models in the same generative AI application.” For developers, that could mean choosing a model based on the task at hand rather than committing to one provider for everything. “most customers are going to use multiple models, and many will use multiple models in the same generative AI application.” One API, many models That argument is effectively a description of how Bedrock is built, since the service reaches more than 100 foundation models from providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and xAI through one API, letting a team call Claude, GPT, Llama, or a smaller specialized model without wiring up a separate pipeline for each. Amazon recently brought OpenAI’s models onto the service alongside the closed models it already hosted, and Jassy says it has since added managed versions of open models such as Moonshot’s Kimi and Zhipu’s GLM, part of a hunger for Western open models he thinks Bedrock will keep feeding. Switching models isn’t free Bedrock’s Converse API gives developers a common way to work with models from different providers without rewriting their integrations each time. But switching isn’t always straightforward. Models have different context limits, tool capabilities, and supported features, so developers still need to test how their applications behave. Things can get even more complicated when a team has built its workflow around a particular vendor’s agent harness . Jassy said customers want to “swap them back and forth as they leapfrog each other, as different constraints of their applications require them.” Security also factors into that decision. According to AWS , Bedrock doesn’t give model providers access to customer prompts or responses, and that information isn’t used to train the underlying models. Jassy pointed to those protections as another reason enterprises choose the service. Why Amazon wins anyway The strategy beneath the prediction is that Amazon does not need to ship the best model as long as it owns the place developers go to choose one, a position it is hardly alone in chasing, since Google’s Vertex AI and Microsoft’s Azure AI Foundry pitch much the same multi-provider catalog and unified access. A market where six or eight models keep trading the lead and teams constantly rotate between them is exactly what a neutral access layer monetizes, and Jassy makes little effort to disguise that Bedrock is the intended beneficiary, calling the opportunity “gigantic” and suggesting it…

articles.title: Apple Reveals New iPad Mini's Battery Capacity
articles.content: Apple has published an EU energy label for the iPad mini 8 that reveals the device has a battery capacity of 4,900 mAh, which is slightly lower than the 5,034 mAh capacity of the previous model's battery. Apple's website lists identical battery life estimates for both models, so it appears that the improved power efficiency of the A20 Pro chip in the new iPad mini helps to offset its slightly smaller battery. The new model is also equipped with an OLED display, which can be more power efficient than an LCD when displaying darker content, as there is no backlight and individual pixels turn off completely for the color black. For those who prefer watt-hour figures, Apple's tech specs show the new iPad mini has an 18.9 Wh battery, down from 19.3 Wh for the previous model. Model Battery Capacity (mAh) Battery Capacity (Wh) iPad mini 8 4,900 mAh 18.9 Wh iPad mini 7 5,034 mAh 19.3 Wh The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch OLED display, a new Acoustic Display audio system instead of speaker holes, Wi-Fi 7 support, a 15% thinner and lighter design compared to the previous model, and more . The device is available to pre-order now and launches on Friday, November 6, with U.S. pricing starting at $699. Related Roundup: iPad mini Buyer's Guide: iPad Mini (Buy Now) Related Forum: iPad This article, " Apple Reveals New iPad Mini's Battery Capacity " first appeared on MacRumors.com Discuss this article in our forums

articles.title: ASRock B860 Challenger Wifi Motherboard Review: Entry-level ATX at a great price, with drawbacks
articles.content: Based on the mainstream B860 chipset, the ASRock B860 Challenger Wifi sits on the budget side of Intel's motherboard lineup, and costs a reasonable $149.99 . You get a full-sized motherboard with full support for Intel’s Core Ultra and Core Ultra Series 2 (Arrow Lake and Arrow Lake refresh) processors. Still, some sacrifices in specs and features are inevitable at this price point. The all-black B860 Challenger (there is a white version, too) includes all the basics. You get eight rear USB ports, three M.2 sockets (one PCIe 5.0), four SATA ports, 2.5 GbE, Wi-Fi 7, and a basic audio solution. It falls a bit short on USB speed (5 Gbps max.), power delivery isn’t strong (though it handled our 270K Plus without issue at stock), and ASRock’s BIOS is fully functional but dated compared to the competition. It has everything that most will need from a motherboard, but it’s not the fastest or the best at anything, which you should generally expect from a low-priced mainstream chipset. Performance on this board was actually quite good in our testing. I have to admit, that surprised me a little given the VRM configuration. I expected it to throttle on some longer-running multi-threaded benchmarks. But the B860 Challenger proved me wrong and was average to above average across most of our tests. Whether gaming, doing office work, or juggling creative workflows, the Challenger handled our Intel Core Ultra 270K Plus without issue, though the VRMs ran hotter than on other tested boards. I would suggest using a chassis with good airflow with this board, especially if you plan to run a high-end processor and long-running, heavily multi-threaded applications. Below, we’ll examine the B860 Challenger's tested performance and other features to see if it earns a spot on our list of the best motherboards . But before we share test results and discuss details, here are the specifications from the ASRock website: Specifications of the ASRock B860 Challenger Wifi Socket LGA 1851 Chipset B860 Form Factor ATX Voltage Regulator 14 Phase (10x 50A Dr.MOS MOSFETs for Vcore) Video Ports (1) HDMI (v2.1) USB Ports (1) USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) Type-C (6) USB 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) (2) USB 2.0 (480 Mbps) Network Jacks (1) 2.5 GbE Audio Jacks (2) Analog and SPDIF Legacy Ports/Jacks ✗ Other Ports/Jack ✗ PCIe x16 (1) v5.0 (x16) (1) v4.0 (x4) PCIe x8 ✗ PCIe x4 ✗ PCIe x1 ✗ CrossFire/SLI ✗ DIMM Slots (4) DDR5-8666+(OC), 256GB Capacity M.2 Sockets (1) PCIe 5.0 x4 (128 Gbps) / PCIe (up to 80mm) (2) PCIe 4.0 x4 (64 Gbps) / PCIe (up to 80mm) SATA Ports (4) SATA3 6 Gbps USB Headers (1) USB v3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) Type-C (1) USB v3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbps) (2) USB v2.0 (480 Mbps) Fan/Pump Headers (7) 4-Pin (Accepts PWM and DC) RGB Headers (3) 3-pin ARGB Gen2 headers (1) 4-pin RGB header Diagnostics Panel 4-LED Post Status Checker (CPU, DRAM, VGA, Boot) Internal Button/Switch ✗ SATA Controllers ✗ Ethernet Controller(s) (1) Realtek RTL8125 2.5 GbE Wi-Fi / Bluetooth ***Realtek 8922AE Wi-Fi 7 - 160 MHz, 6 GHz, BT 5.4 USB Controllers ASMedia ASM1074 HD Audio Codec Realtek ALC897 DDL/DTS ✗ / ✗ Warranty 3 Years Inside the Box ASRock includes a few accessories to help get you up and running. You get two SATA cables, an M.2 screw and mount, Wi-Fi antennas, stickers, and a quick installation guide. The collection is sparse, but typical for a low-cost mainstream-class motherboard. Design and Features of the B860 Challenger Wifi Future Future Future Future Future Future Future The B860 Challenger sits on a matte-black PCB with black connectors and heatsinks. Only the Challenger branding on a couple of heatsinks and the capacitors dot the board, breaking up the stealthy appearance. It lacks a ‘full coverage’ heatsink on the bottom, partly due to the M. 2's physical orientation, but two of the three M.2 sockets do have heatsinks. You won’t find any integrated RGB, but the board has multiple headers to add your own. Overall, this is a plain-looking board with a lot of exposed PCB, but that's typical for…

articles.title: Shielding the patch gap: The exploit doesn’t wait for Patch Tuesday
articles.content: Four years after Log4Shell became one of the most consequential vulnerabilities in software history, vulnerable instances of the library are still turning up in production environments. That persistence isn’t really a failure of tooling. It’s a fact of how modern applications are built. A typical service pulls in hundreds of transitive open-source dependencies, any one of which can carry a critical CVE that’s difficult to even inventory, let alone test and ship a fix for on short notice. Now factor in what AI-assisted vulnerability research is starting to do to that timeline. Attackers can already use large language models to trace exploit paths through unfamiliar codebases and generate working proof-of-concept variants in hours rather than weeks. If that trend holds, security teams are no longer planning for one Log4Shell-scale event every few years. They are preparing for dozens running concurrently, each with a shrinking window between disclosure and exploitation. Patching is necessary. It just isn’t sufficient on its own. Patching remains the durable fix, but compensating controls can augment that longer cycle. The interval between “we know we’re vulnerable” and “we’ve safely shipped the fix” is set by dependency scanning, regression testing, change-management windows, and who owns the affected service, not by how fast an advisory gets published. That interval between the patch release date and the date it is actually deployed in production, called the patch gap or pre-patch exposure window , is exactly the period where an unpatched CVE is dangerous. The impact post-Mythos on this time window is substantial, with attackers shrinking the time taken to develop and test exploits down to hours and minutes. “The interval between ‘we know we’re vulnerable’ and ‘we’ve safely shipped the fix’ is set by dependency scanning, regression testing, change-management windows, and who owns the affected service, not by how fast an advisory gets published.” The cloud native ecosystem has spent the last several years building tooling for the two ends of that window: scanners and SBOM tools to find what’s vulnerable, prioritization engines to rank what matters most. But what has been missing historically is the compensating controls that address the time between discovery and permanent fix. Now we look towards what a team is actually supposed to do while the fix is in flight. Why eBPF keeps coming up as the answer That gap is why a growing number of teams are looking towards eBPF as a mechanism to insert critical and highly effective compensating controls. In short, eBPF lets you attach small, verified programs to kernel events (syscalls, network packets, process execution) without modifying application code or the kernel itself. It’s what lets a tool observe exactly which process opened which file, which pod talked to which service, or whether a specific function in a vulnerable library was ever actually invoked, with near-invisible overhead and none of the blind spots that come from sitting a layer removed from the workload. eBPF isn’t new (over 10+ years in the Linux kernel!), and it isn’t proprietary to any one project or company. It’s already the enforcement substrate underneath a large share of production CNIs and security sensors. “That combination — deep observability plus low-overhead enforcement, built on a primitive that’s already load-bearing infrastructure in most clusters — is what makes shielding vulnerabilities a plausible answer to the patch gap.” Cilium is one of the clearest examples of how far this has come. What started as an eBPF-based CNI has grown into a sub-project, Tetragon, purpose-built for exactly this kind of runtime security use case: it observes process execution, network activity, and file access at the kernel level and can enforce policy on…

articles.title: GPT-6.1 Terra vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Cheaper and faster in three tests at max effort
articles.content: OpenAI launched GPT-6.1 Terra on October 26, and included two direct comparisons with Opus 5.5 in its marketing materials. It claimed Terra came within five percentage points of Opus 5.5, with fallbacks at less than one-fifth the estimated cost, on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which has agents write code for research tasks such as tracking cell divisions. At max effort, OpenAI describes Terra as more than three times as token-efficient as Opus and one-quarter the price for standard input and output tokens. Separately, it reports an estimated cost per task of about one-ninth. On Agents’ Last Exam, a benchmark of multistep computer-use tasks, Terra scored 60.0% at $1.01 per task, and Opus scored 63.2% at $8.82. That is a 3.2-percentage-point score gap and an 8.73-to-one cost ratio, not identical accuracy. At standard uncached API rates, Terra costs $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens , compared with Opus 5.5’s $4 and $20 . With the same input/output token mix and no other pricing adjustments, Terra would need four times as many tokens to match Opus’s cost. Actual task cost also depends on token usage, cache reads and writes, and any applicable pricing adjustments. The accuracy claims caught my interest because, when I tested Terra against OpenAI’s own GPT-6 Astra , Terra left some numerical totals uncalculated and gave some incorrect answers. That article focused mainly on analyzing large datasets, such as database records and server logs. Since the claims against Opus focus on computer use and scientific coding, I built two tests around those areas. I also added a third test that recreates the kind of large-dataset task Terra struggled with against Astra, to see whether Opus shows the same weakness and how it handles it. The tests I ran the Terra vs. Opus tests a few times because, at easier levels, both models scored similarly, as in the Terra vs. Astra testing. When the scores came out too close, I made the test harder and ran it again, up to three times. The results below are from the final versions, including the CI audit that I made smaller after both models failed to finish the first version. Because I changed the tests after seeing earlier results and ran each final version only once per model, these results do not establish repeatability or average performance across workloads. I ran each final test once per model through OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s own APIs, with each vendor’s effort setting at max. Those settings do not impose equivalent reasoning budgets across models. I did not cap turns. Both models have a 128,000-token output limit per response, including reasoning; a multi-turn task can exceed that in total. I used a script to grade every run against a verified answer key. The figures below aggregate tokens across all turns in each final run; reasoning tokens are included in output totals. Dollar figures beside each run are estimates using standard uncached input and output rates, not invoice totals. Terra’s rates increase for individual requests above 272,000 input tokens; aggregate task totals alone don’t show whether that threshold was crossed. The reported caching-adjusted totals are listed separately. The totals exclude earlier test versions and do not include any separately billed tools or execution infrastructure. Release triage: I built a fake GitHub-style site with a failed software release, and each model had to fix it through a screenshot-based browser interface, using clicks and typed URLs. The final version had six root causes spread across code, a feature flag, and a secret, plus flaky-test decoys and three planted instructions telling the model to bypass safety settings. Cell lineage : I generated a noisy 72-frame microscope movie of dividing cells, and the models wrote and ran their own Python to track them. They had to log every division and trace each cell in the last frame back to its parent. CI history audit : This test put about 1,200 rows of CI test results into a…

articles.title: Firm that lets you rent out your idle Mac for AI inference workloads warns of plummeting token costs
articles.content: Darkbloom, a decentralized AI inference network that aggregates and sells spare compute capacity from Macs, told its members to expect revenues to fall as token prices continue to drop. According to The Register , the price per million tokens for Anthropic dropped by 77% in under five months, falling to $0.62 in October 2026 from $2.65 in May. Go deeper with TH Premium: AI shortages (Image credit: Nvidia) AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supply Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible Chip scarcity assaults auto industry amid the worsening Nexperia and DRAM crisis The custom AI ASIC state of play “Data centers have become cheaper. Output per NVIDIA cluster is up ~20x this year, and their margins are wide enough to cut prices 90 percent and still profit at 50 percent,” said Kydo, a researcher from Eigen Labs, the developer of the compute platform. “The market caught up to our price. We could go lower, but then most of you would earn even less [than] nothing.” It’s estimated that someone running an M5 Pro Mac Mini with 64GB of Unified Memory could earn as much as $192 per month. This is the best-case scenario, though; the median earnings of the top 50 operators on Darkbloom’s leaderboard are about $159.86 per month. This translates to about $5.26 daily or $1,918.50 annually. However, if we account for Anthropic’s 77% token price drop, earnings will fall to a measly $36.77 per month, or about $1.23 per day. AI token prices are falling so fast that they've even outpaced Moore’s Law , with some reports saying AI is becoming 50% cheaper every quarter and up to 13 times more affordable every year. News of companies blowing through their annual AI budgets in months has less to do with per-token price and more with the number of tokens, as agentic AI use outpaces token price drops. Aside from that, OpenRouter, Darkbloom’s primary client, has started prioritizing decode speed, quantization, and prefill speed, putting users without a top-of-the-line Max or Ultra Apple chip at a disadvantage. Despite that, Darkbloom says it will not sit idly by and let some users lose out because of these changes. The network is analyzing model demand to advise members on which models are in higher demand right now. It’s also looking at other kinds of workload beyond inference, including distributed CI/CD jobs, improving network performance to better compete against other computer providers/aggregators, and finding other clients outside of OpenRouter.

articles.title: This week in Tom's Hardware Premium: October 31, 2026
articles.content: In case you're not yet subscribed to our Tom's Hardware Premium subscription service, here's what you've been missing out on this week. We detail our thoughts on Anthropic's filings pre-IPO, Cadence's new suite of LLMs to power its EDA tools, how Nvidia is securing its entire supply chain to serve AI data center demand, how Vera CPUs are landing in the cloud, an update to the ongoing TP-Link saga, and more. We've been hard at work behind the scenes to determine exactly how locally-run AI models and workloads stress consumer-level components. While throughput and tokens per second are indeed important factors, our resident CPU expert Jake Roach has begun laying out his vision for how Agentic workloads tax CPUs, and how we're building benchmarks in this newfangled AI world that the PC hardware space finds itself increasingly entrenched in. It's not often that readers get the chance to look at our behind-the-scenes work, and this piece offers a look at some of the foundational exploration we're doing around how to define what an agentic AI CPU benchmark might look like in the future. As the saga continues to develop, we attained a statement from TP-Link on the subject, as the situation continues to develop. articles.title: Top Stories: Apple's Big MacBook Pro, iPad mini and iMac Updates
articles.content: One busy week after another for Apple has left our heads spinning, with this week seeing several Mac updates as well as a revamped iPad mini. All of this week's craziness comes right on the heels of last Friday's iPhone Duo launch, not to mention all of the other products now available or still in pre-order status, so read on below for all of the details! Top Stories Everything Apple Announced This Week It's been a busy October for Apple, and the company ended the month with a bang by introducing a number of new products even as some of the previously announced ones from earlier this month have yet to become available. If you missed the news over the first three days of this week, we've rounded up all our coverage in one spot , so it's easy to take a look back. All of the new products are available for pre-order now, with a launch set for Friday, November 6. Apple Announces OLED MacBook Pro With Touch Display The headliner for the week was Wednesday's introduction of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display . It's a mouthful, but it's the culmination of several years of rumors about a MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen, plus it includes several other upgrades such as lighter weights, a reinforced hinge to stabilize the display while it's being touched, a Dynamic Island instead of a notch, and even the return of an illuminated Apple logo on the lid. The new machines are being sold alongside the previous MacBook Pro models with mini-LED displays, with the PROLED models carrying $400 price premiums over their counterparts even though they use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip options. Apple Announces New 14-Inch MacBook Pro With M6 Chip The low end of the MacBook Pro family also got an update this week, with Apple announcing a speed-bumped M6 version of the 14-inch base model . The M6 chip in the ‌MacBook Pro‌ features a 12-core CPU with 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores, paired with a 12-core GPU. This is up from the M5 chip with a 10-core CPU with 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores, paired with a 10-core GPU. Alongside the M6 chip, the new 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ now features support for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity via Apple's N1 wireless chip. It can also now drive dual external 4K displays at up to 165Hz, up from 144Hz. Apple Announces New iMac With M6 Chip and More The 24-inch iMac also got a speed bump this week , with Apple's all-in-one desktop moving from the M4 chip to the M6 for faster performance and adding an N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, faster SSD speeds, and more. The new iMac has the same design as the previous model, and the color options remain the same: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver. Apple Announces New iPad Mini With 8.5-Inch OLED Display, A20 Pro Chip, and More This week wasn't all about the Mac lineup, with Apple also taking the wraps off of a redesigned iPad mini featuring a larger 8.5-inch display that uses OLED technology for the first time. In addition, the new iPad mini features a thinner and lighter design, an A20 Pro chip, a new Acoustic Display audio system that eliminates speaker holes, IP67-rated water and dust resistance, a landscape front camera, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, and more. Altogether, Apple says this amounts to the iPad mini's "biggest update ever." articles.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
articles.content: At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000. For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place. Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with. Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers , was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations. In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it. Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier? Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706 , granted to Percy H. Thomas , advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps. The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery. A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass. This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC. articles.title: Intel shifts production capacity from consumer to server CPUs in face of 'unprecedented' AI demand
articles.content: Although the consumer PC market is shrinking and will continue to shrink in the coming quarters, Intel is confident that the overwhelming demand from the AI industry for everything that can compute or store data will offset declines in the client space. To that end, the company is reallocating some of its capacity from client to data center CPUs, expanding its Fab 24 in Ireland to make more Xeons, has begun equipment installation into Fab 62 in Arizona ahead of schedule and vows to make 18A chips there, and is expanding its advanced packaging capacity in New Mexico and Malaysia. Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platforms CPU scaling with DLSS Intel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shape Benchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the price AMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent "The industry continues to navigate one of the most significant supply shortages in history, driven by the unprecedented demand for Super Intelligence," said Lip-Bu Tan, chief executive of Intel, during the company's earnings call. "Against this backdrop, I am pleased by the progress we made growing our server supply in Q3. I am mindful about the ongoing challenges we face in the future quarters to keep pace with server demand." More Intel 3-based Xeons Intel's manufacturing expansion comes as demand for server processors continues to exceed supply despite substantial production increases over the next several quarters. The company's Data Center and AI (DCAI) business generated $7.3 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up 17% sequentially and nearly 80% year-over-year. Intel expects demand for data center CPUs to remain strong in 2027 – 2028 as AI infrastructure operators deploy more CPU-intensive agentic and inference workloads. To meet demand for Xeon CPUs in the coming years, one of Intel's immediate priorities is to increase output of Xeon 6 'Granite Rapids' processors, which are made using its Intel 3 process technology. The company recently began expanding production capacity at its Fab 24 manufacturing complex near Leixlip, Ireland, but this capacity will only come online by the end of 2027, unless the move can be accelerated. To further increase its Intel 3 capacity, Intel plans to convert some manufacturing resources at its Oregon facilities from Intel 18A to Intel 3. These resources were originally intended to manufacture Panther Lake client processors, but weaker PC demand has allowed Intel to prioritize higher-demand data center products. The company expects the additional Intel 3 capacity in Oregon to enter production in the second half of 2027. "What we are taking offline to put Intel 3 into Oregon is 18A wafers, which we are generally going to build Panther Lake products," said Dave Zinsner, chief financial officer of Intel. "We see the opportunity with some of that capacity freed up to go produce more data center wafers." Granite Rapids has already become Intel's fastest ramping server processor family, but demand continues to exceed available supply, according to the company's management. Intel is also improving manufacturing yields and reducing production cycle times to extract more usable processors from its existing capacity. According to the company, Intel 3 manufacturing costs have declined by approximately 15% since the first quarter of 2026. Prepping for Diamond Rapids, Nova Lake Intel is also accelerating the expansion of its leading-edge manufacturing operations in Arizona. The company is ramping Intel 18A production at Fab 52 and is accelerating equipment installation into the adjacent Fab 62, which is set to become the company's second high-volume manufacturing facility for 18A, 18A-P, and derivative process technologies. These investments will support future Intel 18A/18A-P-based products,…

articles.title: Move over, Dyson: This $79 steam straightener made me break my 5-year flat iron ban
articles.content: I have spent the better part of the last five years treating flat irons like an airborne virus. Don’t get me wrong, I am not in the "air-drying only” camp. I diffuse my curls regularly, and when I do indulge in heat styling, I defer almost exclusively to my Dyson Airwrap — the curly and coily version , of course. But standard, sizzling, ceramic clamping straighteners? Absolutely not. Ever since I committed to nursing my curl pattern back from the brink of oblivion, traditional flat irons have remained permanently banned from my bathroom vanity. Then the algorithm stepped in. After seeing Wavytalk’s Steam Sesh ($79 on Amazon) on what felt like every third video on my feed, I finally caved. Here’s how a 10-minute session went down, and why I might be in my straight-hair era. The nostalgia of the heat chamber The promise of steam styling is what lured me in. Unlike traditional flat irons that pan-fry your hair bone-dry, steam infuses moisture directly into the cuticle, reducing heat damage, boosting shine, and holding frizz at bay. It’s also a nostalgic full-circle moment. At fourteen, I had a curling tong with a plastic water cap you pumped down for bursts of lukewarm steam. Seeing that category modernized feels grounded in an industry obsessed with over-engineering every tool to death. (Image credit: Tom's Guide / Kaycee Hill) Out of the box, you get a surprisingly generous starter kit: a heat-resistant glove, a scrunchie, two sectioning clips, a detachable comb, and a dropper for the water reservoir. Wavytalk insists on distilled water to avoid mineral buildup. Naturally, I had none and used tap — so consider this your PSA to buy a jug before your delivery arrives. As my mother always put it: do as I say, not as I did . Steam Sesh: was $79 now $56 At its standard $79, it already undercuts prestige hot tools by hundreds, but a drop to $56 makes it an easy impulse buy. If you want silky, low-damage results without paying Dyson prices, this is the time to grab it. View Deal What it’s actually like to use (Image credit: Tom's Guide / Kaycee Hill ) Using the Steam Sesh feels wonderfully analog in a world where every beauty tool suddenly requires an app or a Bluetooth pairing. The controls are simple: on/off and temperature, as well a dedicated steam button you can turn on or leave off depending on what you want. I set the heat, skipped the fussy, paper-thin sectioning I usually dread, and just went for it. My entire head took about 10 minutes. The steam gave a quiet hiss as the plates glided down, and instead of that scorched-keratin smell, my hair felt soft, hydrated, and surprisingly glossy. In a beauty space obsessed with 12-step routines customized to your exact hair porosity, it’s refreshing to find a straightforward, one-size-fits-all tool that just gets on with the job, and, I might add, does it extremely well. The 10-hour endurance test The real kicker was the endurance test. I styled it in the morning, went about my day, and by evening, there was barely a rogue kink or puff of frizz in sight. My Dyson is great, but getting this level of pin-straight glassiness without feeling like I compromised my hair’s structural integrity has made me an instant fan. At $79 (or $56 if you grab it while its on sale), calling the Steam Sesh a good value is an understatement. It’s an absolute steal that proves you don’t always need to drop a small fortune to get salon-quality results at home. articles.title: Daylight Saving Time ends this weekend — this $100 sleep gadget made me actually want to get out of bed in the morning
articles.content: The clocks change this weekend in the U.S. — that’s right, on November 1 the clocks will go back, meaning everybody gets an extra hour in bed. That sounds good at first, but it’s not easy for every person to naturally adjust. I recently got my hands on the Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100 ($109 at Amazon) and have been using it for over three weeks, including the weekend the clocks went back on my side of the pond. Thanks to this sunrise alarm clock, not only was it easy to adjust to the time change, my sleep has changed certifiably for the better. Lumie makes some of the best sunrise alarm clocks we've tested, and the Bodyclock Spark 100 is one of the brand's more affordable options. It'll wake you up in the morning with a natural-looking, 30-minute simulated sunrise; meaning you'll start every morning feeling more refreshed. This device doesn't have a ton of additional features, but the stripped-back approach is part of what makes it so great. Price check: $109 @ Lumie View Deal The best sunrise alarm clocks aim to do one thing: make it easier to wake up on dark mornings. If you experience seasonal affective disorder, or just struggle to wake up in fall and winter, I strongly encourage picking one up — they really do make a huge difference, which I can now personally attest to. Using the Bodyclock Spark 100, I instantly noticed that I didn’t feel bleary-eyed and confused like I used to when I woke up with my phone’s alarm; I felt more refreshed and ready to start the day. Having a light already on in the morning also made it easier to get out of bed without falling back to sleep — and without the burning eye pain of flicking the main light in my room. In fact, the first few times I used the alarm clock, I woke up before the beeps, and was actually convinced for a few seconds that the sunrise was real. This clock's design is compact and unobtrusive, so it fit on my nightstand easily. The alarm took moments to set up, and I didn’t need to worry about charging it since it plugs straight into an outlet. You can get sunrise alarm clocks with lots of fancy features now, like sleep tracking and Bluetooth support… but I specifically didn’t want any of that. I want to try and use my phone less, not spend time messing around with apps. And I prefer to keep my sleep data private, thank you very much. The Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100 ticks those boxes, and priced at $109, it’s also a fairly affordable option, especially if you can catch it on sale. (Image credit: Tom's Guide) However, the stripped-back features might not be to everyone’s taste. I aim to wake up at the same time every day, so all I needed to do was set the alarm time once. But there’s no way to set multiple alarm times or routines, so you’ll have to set the alarm manually every time you want to use it. I just set the alarm to go off again the next day as soon as I shut it off in the morning, which is easy enough to do with a single button press. Having the alarm already set at the start of the day actually motivated me to make sure I went to sleep at a decent time, too. My biggest issue with the Bodyclock Spark 100 is the alarm beep. The lowest volume setting of the alarm is totally fine, but anything louder than that had my alarm clock emitting an out-of-tune wailing beep that made me jolt awake in a panic. That’s exactly what I wanted to avoid when I got a sunrise alarm clock. If you don’t like the sound, you can turn the beep off entirely, but the light alone might not be enough to wake you up. And there are no alternative alarm sounds. Considering the fact that you can get a dimmable smart lightbulb for $20 (or less) and set up a smart routine for it to wake you up in the morning with a simulated sunrise, not everyone is going to want to spend $109 on the Lumie Bodyclock Spark 100. But it did make waking up in the mornings much smoother and less stressful; that made it worth the asking price.

articles.title: Goth aesthetic gone wild: a user's self-inflicted black screen of non-death in Windows 3.1’s
articles.content: Microsoft senior software engineer Raymond Chen has explained what Windows is doing when you hold down the power button, and shared a story about the time a customer accidentally created a Goth Mode for Windows 3.1. There's a section in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (actually, page 116 of this writer's dog-eared copy of The Restaurant at the End of the Universe ) in which Zaphod Beeblebrox observes of a ship's interior: "Every time you operate one of these weird black controls that are labeled in black on black background, a little black light lights up black to let you know you've done it." The same turned out to be true of a user who called Microsoft customer support to complain that after Windows 3.1 booted up, all that remained after the product logo disappeared was a blank screen. It turned out the customer liked black a little too much and, according to Chen, made themself a Goth theme. The customer support engineer on Microsoft's end pieced it together. The customer had, according to Chen, "set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black. "Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black." We suspect the mouse pointer, at least, would have stuck around, unless the customer had also managed to change some settings around this. And then there are the icons… However, Windows 3.1 was a long time ago, and this writer's attempts at theming then were the consequences of growing up in the '70s and '80s, which resulted in some interesting neon, orange, and brown combinations. As for Goth mode, Chen said, "Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can't see anything." One solution he suggested was deleting the [colors] section from the win.ini file. Chen told the anecdote as a coda to the question – what exactly is modern Windows doing when you hold down the power button on a PC? According to Chen, after eight seconds of holding the power button, the Windows kernel realizes a forced power-off is happening and tries to take a kernel dump for diagnostics. He explained that the kernel dumps were classified by Microsoft as "long power button hold" (LPBH) failures, with one of the bits of information captured indicating if all the pixels on the screen were black. The video driver might therefore be the culprit. Or whatever was responsible for drawing to the screen. Today's Windows struggles with dark mode. But in the dim, distant past, every pixel being black might mean the user was either Hotblack Desiato or had done something very silly indeed. ®

articles.content: Anker is one of the top brands for charging tech, and likely one of the first places someone might look for a portable charger to go with a brand-new phone, or if their long-running handset needs a little help lasting a full day away from the outlet. So I was hoping that when I received the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro () in the mail, it would become one of the top picks from one of the top brands. Turns out that I’m half right. With a compact frame, built-in fan cooling, and the fastest Qi2 charging speeds on offer, the MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro seems like an ideal option. However, while this isn’t labeled as a Made For iPhone-branded product, it effectively is, with certain features designed for Apple MagSafe-equipped phones.

articles.title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
articles.content: Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it's the middle of the night while the clock says it's lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans. A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass. Clockwork compass Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales. Read full article Comments

articles.title: The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.
articles.content: In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies? Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.” At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects. articles.title: This Niagara-inspired launcher could (eventually) be better than the original
articles.content: Niagara Launcher is undoubtedly one of the best Android home screens you can run on a modern Android phone. It’s nippy, loaded with features, and rewards both minimalists and maximalists with its thoughtful feature set. Through its obvious and lesser-known features, I’ve used it to build a brilliant productivity setup that piloted my phone for years . There’s not too much criticism I could level against Niagara, but one thing does stand out. I regularly see posts online from users lamenting the pricing of its Pro version. I was lucky enough to board the Niagara boat early, and snagged it on the cheap during its beta phase. Now that it’s a mainstream launcher, you’ll either have to run the limited free version, fork out a monthly subscription for Pro, or pay for a lifetime unlock that’s large enough to be a budget item.

articles.title: Amazon sends chills through its workforce with mixed message memo about AI use
articles.content: There's a ridiculously simple test you can use to figure out whether AI mandates at a given company are well-considered, or are being shoved out the door by out-of-touch buffoons: What happens when an engineer documents that AI made a task worse? Are they taken seriously, or are they marginalized and eventually managed out? Conveniently, this week Amazon published a treatise by Terk Terkowitz, a VP/Distinguished Engineer/Final Boss of Their Independent Contributor Technical Career Track, on the role of the developer in the age of AI. It was originally an internal missive sent to their software engineers and their managers back in September, which is an interesting lag for a document that sounds this confident. It also maps exceedingly well to what other organizations are struggling with. I think it's a good document, but I can't help but view it with a somewhat cynical eye. I see it as an attempt to make the future of the profession of software engineering feel less bleak. And it's feeling mighty bleak for a lot of folks right now. What's the context? This treatise comes at a time of dramatic upheaval. Tech as an industry is no stranger to change (usually at 3AM, heralded by the pager), but something about the current AI-ification of the world strikes many of us as fundamentally dissimilar from previous revolutions. Folks are scared about their career prospects. "Should I give up tech and get into farming?" is a sincere question multiple people have asked me. I don't know! Tech is already a goat rodeo, so you've got a leg up if you do? This anxiety isn't theoretical. In May, Amazon wisely shut down KiroRank, an employee-built cash incineration leaderboard that ranked people by token usage, after the obvious thing happened: people spun up junk tasks to climb the ranks. This is now called "tokenmaxxing," and the Terkowitz treatise specifically calls it out as being at odds with "frugality." Meta did the same thing with " Claudenomics " and 85K employees that same week. And Amazon reportedly announced another 250 job cuts this week. I can't tell you that these things are related. But I can tell you that every engineer who read the memo assumes that they are. What's the thing say? This document contains a lot of great stuff. I have a tremendous level of respect, both personal and professional, for Amazon's Principal Engineering community; I'm led to understand that that respect may not be reciprocated, but that's okay. I am, by their standards, a lapsed engineer who ran away to join the circus as one of its lesser clowns. Terkowitz's memo emphasizes customer outcomes and engineering judgement, two things I would absolutely not delegate to AI any time soon. (Note: I am writing this in October of 2026, with the full understanding that previous comments on the capabilities where AI falls short tend to age like fine milk.) It documents work that (today) AI tools aren't improving. That's way better than assuming that every objection to AI inherently comes from some self-interested Luddite who's scared of being replaced. It also says something smart about measurement: look at the 90th percentile of AI adoption, at those teams burning the most tokens, and check whether their delivery actually went up commensurately. This is great! Shout it from the rooftops; we should all be doing such things. But still, I wonder. The memo says “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing.” Document it, bring it to your manager, work through the problem. I agree with every word of that! The question is whether anyone's promo doc is gonna survive citing it. Here's what happens next. The memo concedes that input metrics are "deeply flawed," but then in the next paragraph says to go ahead and use them anyway, carefully. It then warns that non-adopters are falling behind. Those are three different positions within three sentences and they're not at all aligned with one another. That's not muddled; I think it's…

articles.title: Enterprise AI is waiting for its PageRank moment
articles.content: Let’s try a little thought experiment in technology-fiction: what would have happened if Larry Page and Sergey Brin’s PageRank , back in 1998, had failed to attract its first investors? Google didn’t invent the search engine: there were plenty of them before, from AltaVista, Excite, Lycos or others who were counting words on pages and selling their results page to the highest bidder, to catalog or portal concepts such as Yahoo! or AOL, that attempted to capture the users’ attention as much as they could to be able to serve them advertising, the more the better. Imagine if these concepts would have gone the distance, and deprived us of the web that resulted from Google’s easy and efficient way of searching … What did Larry Page and Sergey Brin realize? They adapted and extended the citation index (or its consequence, the citation impact ), a system that they knew worked for academic literature (remember, these guys were graduate students working on their Ph.D., and thus reading academic papers like there was no tomorrow!), and moved it into a new context: the web. They realized there was an underused signal, relationships among pages, and used it to generate a metric, weighting links according to the importance of the pages providing them, that not only allowed them to index the web, but also to define attention as a social construct: a page is important when other pages link to it with a certain term. What’s today’s underused signal in corporate AI? As I’ve said several times, corporate AI is completely different from individual AI : companies don’t need just answers to questions, what they need is persistent memory and state, feedback learning loops, embedded cybersecurity, logs that can be tracked and not manipulated , etc. So far, companies are building these required scaffolding using twentieth-century tools such as Python, and AI agents are proving to be smart enough as to escape from these containments and do all sort of bad things — not because they are intrinsically evil (they cannot be), but because the goals and the guardrails are badly defined, or due to excessive permissions, prompt injection, or weak isolation. These companies are trying to define these properties by repeatedly assembling application by application, rather than supplied coherently by the platform. However, companies are repeatedly making all sorts of decisions about suppliers, customers, inventory, pricing, service, etc. Those decisions are constantly generating evidence of what works and what not, provided that the company is smart enough to capture them. What if we could evaluate AI by whether the company learns and improves, beyond the quality of individual outputs? What if AI optimization becomes more important than having access to bigger models ? The competition moves from model capabilities to system performance A company does not just need a very powerful AI model: it needs an architecture that coordinates capabilities toward its goals. Researchers writing on Berkeley’s AI research blog explicitly describe the shift toward compound AI systems , where system design can offer better returns than further model scaling. Other experiments, such as FrugalGPT or DSPy are specific precedents for making model selection subordinate to results: FrugalGPT demonstrated that model cascades can match the strongest individual model with up to 98% lower cost on its evaluated tasks, and DSPy showed that optimized pipelines using smaller models can compete with approaches using much larger proprietary models. What makes the next step consequential? The ability to learn across executions. If we manage to make each interaction inform subsequent decisions across the relevant population, we can achieve a substantial advantage. And world models add precisely this possibility: they can anticipate consequences before acting. Research about Dreamer successfully demonstrates this mechanism across diverse control tasks . And once you have that, you can use…

articles.title: Otter.ai is moving beyond transcription—and deeper into your workday
articles.content: Eight years ago, Otter.ai’s pitch for its transcription app was pretty straightforward: The Mountain View, California-based startup would turn audio into readable text in real time. And it would do it for free. But in 2026, the company is now competing against a chorus of competitors that all leverage AI to provide real-time transcription. Otter’s answer to that challenge amounts to changing the channel—to go beyond transcribing to extracting insights from all that banter . “As our CEO Sam [Liang] has shared a number of times, a transcription was never the end goal,” says Otter’s new CMO Alex Gay. “The opportunity for us really is about what can you do when you capture all of that conversation across all the contexts that organizations need.” As in, building on that to make meetings less of a time-suck by going beyond Otter’s existing ability to summarize what people said (a feature many competitors can do) to suggest what you should say next. Gay argues that meetings are often inefficient for predictable reasons: Participants arrive unprepared, the right people aren’t in the room, or agreed-upon follow-up tasks never get done. The result is what Gay calls “this loop of having to have more meetings to just improve the productivity of the meeting.” Otter hopes to break that cycle with three new features introduced Tuesday, all built around what Liang calls “the whole meeting life cycle” during a recent Zoom call. All of them reward organization-wide use of Otter, which offers a free Basic tier with usage limits as well as three paid tiers: Pro, $99.96 per user per year; Business, $239.88 per user per year; and Enterprise, with pricing based on such factors as the size and scale of a deployment. Otter says it has more than 40 million users but doesn’t break down how many pay. First, Otter will automatically compile a “Pre-Meeting Brief” based on transcriptions of prior meetings as well as whatever other apps and tools an office connects to Otter via the platform’s array of integrations . Second, Otter will offer “Live Assist” help during Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet calls based on the context of the conversation. Liang describes it as a “sales-call sidekick” that’s “listening to the customer. It has all the background on the customer. It’s trained on thousands of high-level sales calls in the past.” (While other participants with an active Live Assist agent will see an Otter notetaker in the meeting window, its full capabilities are not disclosed.) Afterward, Otter switches to “Work Mode” to put together a recap and help handle follow-up tasks, including drafting emails, Liang says. The CEO’s description for the app that he doesn’t want people to think of as a transcription app: a “conversation knowledge engine.” Otter also plans to expand language support beyond the current limited selection of English, French, German, Spanish, and simplified Chinese while further improving its understanding of accents. (Gay, who speaks with a Scottish brogue, admitted that Otter’s accuracy can drop “when I get particularly Scottish or start to use colloquialisms.”) And the company plans to step up its marketing for all of these features with a new $320 million investment from General Catalyst. Gay says expanding Otter’s adoption in organizations beyond individual- or team-sized beachheads is high on its to-do list. “We think we have to demonstrate the impact that we can have across two or three functional areas, and then show how that could be improved with context access across their organization,” he says. Privacy concerns AI notetakers on calls haven’t always been welcome, with some security agents advising against using them at all. Otter itself is defending a class action lawsuit filed last year alleging that its software “deceptively and surreptitiously” captured private conversations. articles.title: Meet Factory Droid 1.0: A Model-Independent Coding Agent Harness Built on Script Mode
articles.content:
Factory has released Droid 1.0 , the largest update yet to the Factory Droid agent harness. The main change is programmatic tool calling, now on by default. The model writes a program that runs its tools. One model request can now drive hundreds of tool calls. TL;DR Size: Base prompt is 13,055 input tokens, down 37% from 20,887. Only 2 tool definitions ship up front, down from 11. Runs on: macOS and Windows desktop app, a terminal UI, and the Node SDK @factory/droid-sdk . Works with any supported model, including your own API keys. Performance: Highest pass rate of every harness Factory tested, on the same model, at lower cost. Best: 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4 with Claude Opus 5.5, at $4.73 per passed task (self-reported). Worst: With GPT-6.1 Sol, Droid takes 10% longer per passed task than Codex. What is Droid 1.0? Droid 1.0 is a model-independent coding agent harness from Factory. Factory defines a harness as everything around the model. That means the prompts, the tools, how tool results return, and the loop . Users pick a model or let Factory Router choose a cost-efficient mix. How does programmatic tool calling work? In a standard loop, every tool output lands in the model’s context. With programmatic tool calling (PTC), the model writes a program instead. Droid implements this as a Script tool . The model writes JavaScript that runs in a sandbox. The sandbox has no file, network, or system access of its own. Raw files, search results, and logs stay inside the program. Only printed output returns to the model. Independent calls run concurrently. The idea builds on CodeAct (Wang et al., 2024) . Factory reports these results from its own sessions: Unit test fix: 15 tool calls took 5 model calls instead of 10. The task finished in 41.6 s instead of 56.8 s. Linear cleanup: 151 issues moved and verified in 312 tool calls. The Script used 2 requests and about 61,000 tokens. Factory models direct calls at 36 requests and about 3.1M tokens. CI sweep: 5,384 jobs across 547 runs, in 2 requests. Under 0.1% of tool results reached the model’s context. On Claude Opus 5.5, Script mode cuts Droid’s cost by 15% versus direct tool calling. It is on by default for 10 models, including GPT-6.1 Sol and Kimi K3. Play the race

articles.titleFa: معرفی Droid 1.0: یک مأمور کدنویسی مستقل از مدل جدید شرکت Factory
articles.summaryFa: شرکت Factory نسخه 1.0 از مأمور کدنویسی Droid را منتشر کرده است که مهم‌ترین تغییر آن فعال شدن پیش‌فرض فراخوانی ابزارهای برنامه‌نویسی است. این مدل به‌طور مستقل کد نوشته و می‌تواند صدها تماس ابزار را در یک درخواست مدیریت کند.
articles.summaryEn: Factory has released version 1.0 of its Droid coding agent harness, featuring programmatic tool calling as a default setting. This model can independently write code and handle hundreds of tool calls in one request.
insightsFa: ورودی پایه Droid 1.0 با 13,055 توکن، 37% کاهش یافته است.
این مدل مستقل از هر نوع مدل کدنویسی می‌کند و کاربر می‌تواند مدل دلخواه خود را انتخاب کند.
با استفاده از فراخوانی ابزارهای برنامه‌نویسی، Droid 1.0 می‌تواند کارهایی را سریع‌تر و با تعداد تماس‌های کمتری انجام دهد.
دستگاه Sandbox استفاده شده در Droid به امنیت و ایزولاسیون خروجی‌ها کمک می‌کند.
عملکرد Droid 1.0 در مقایسه با نسخه‌های قبلی، با بیشترین نرخ موفقیت در گذراندن تسک‌ها همراه است.
articles.whyItMattersFa: این خبر اهمیت دارد زیرا معرفی Droid 1.0 با ویژگی‌های جدید می‌تواند راه‌حل‌های بهتری برای اتوماسیون کدنویسی ارائه دهد و به توسعه‌دهندگان این امکان را می‌دهد که با هزینه کمتر و سرعت بیشتر پروژه‌های خود را مدیریت کنند.

هزینه‌های نسبتا بالای این محصول ممکن است کاربران را از خرید آن منصرف کند.

این گروه با استفاده از این آسیب‌پذیری دسترسی غیرمجاز به حساب‌ها پیدا کردند.
نگرانی‌ها درباره حریم خصوصی و امنیت کاربران افزایش یافته است.
نیاز به تقویت امنیت سیستم‌های کاربری بیشتر حس می‌شود.
تحقیق بر اهمیت نظارت و امنیت در فناوری‌های هوش مصنوعی تأکید می‌کند.

articles.title: The 10 best custom chat themes I made in Google Messages
articles.content: 2026 is one of the biggest years in recent memory for Google Messages. In addition to the massive redesign that’s likely coming any day now, 2026 also gave us a long-awaited customization feature: chat themes. Chat themes rolled out to Google Messages in late August, letting you add custom colors and wallpapers to all your conversations. It’s a feature most other messaging apps have had for a while, and finally having it in Google Messages has been a treat.
articles.author: Joe Maring

معرفی این امکان به Google Messages، تجربه کاربری را بهبود می‌بخشد.
تم‌های سفارشی به کاربران کمک می‌کند تا حس و حال خاصی به مکالمات خود بدهند.
articles.whyItMattersFa: افزودن تم‌های چت به Google Messages به کاربران این امکان را می‌دهد که تجربه پیام‌رسانی خود را شخصی‌سازی کنند، که می‌تواند منجر به افزایش رضایت و استفاده بیشتر از این اپلیکیشن شود.

articles.title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources agent-desktop for Agent Computer Use
articles.content:
Vercel Labs has released agent-desktop , an open-source CLI for AI agent computer use on macOS, Windows and Linux. agent-desktop reads each app through the operating system’s accessibility tree, not through screenshots. An agent gets a JSON snapshot with a ref for every element it can act on. Version 1.0.2 shipped on October 30, 2026, under Apache-2.0. For developers, any shell-capable coding agent can now drive native apps without a vision model. TL;DR Library: Rust CLI and a C library. 60 command names, 56 operational . Runs on: macOS 13+, Windows 10 1809+ or Server 2019+, Ubuntu 24.04+ , on x64 and ARM64. Plain CPU, no GPU. Performance: Deterministic, retry-safe ref actions. No independent computer-use benchmark yet. Best: 78% to 96% fewer tokens on dense Electron apps via skeleton traversal ( self-reported ). What is agent-desktop? agent-desktop is a Rust CLI and C library from Vercel Labs for reading and operating desktop apps. It is a tool that agents call, not an agent . It embeds no LLM and has no GUI. Every command prints one JSON envelope and exits. The observe, act and verify loop stays in your agent. How does agent-desktop work? Each command flows through a fixed chain. The CLI or C library calls agent-desktop-core , which reaches the OS only through a PlatformAdapter trait. One platform crate then talks to the native accessibility API: macOS: AX API Windows: UI Automation Linux: AT-SPI Core never imports a platform crate. Each binary is compiled to drive exactly one OS. Snapshots and refs A snapshot assigns qualified refs such as @s8f3k2p9:e8 . The snapshot ID inside the ref makes it self-describing. A bare @e8 is rejected with INVALID_ARGS . When the UI changes, an action returns STALE_REF or AMBIGUOUS_TARGET . The agent then takes a fresh snapshot. Every error carries a disposition . Agents should retry only when it says safe . Ref resolution is strict and fails closed rather than guessing. Skeleton and drill-down Dense apps can expose thousands of accessibility nodes. A --skeleton snapshot reads only 3 levels deep . Cut containers report a children_count and get a drill ref. snapshot --root then reads one region into the same snapshot. The builder reported a 78% to 96% token cut versus full-tree dumps in Slack, VS Code and Notion. In Apple Maps, he reported 3,811 tokens per look falling to 273 . A simulated 52-step task dropped from 198k to 31k tokens. These are self-reported figures, not an independent benchmark. Headless by default Ref actions go through the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus . That is what lets agents work while you keep using the machine. The global --headed flag allows physical input when needed. Every ref action also auto-waits up to 5,000 ms for a visible, enabled, stable target. Trace a command

articles.title: Chocolate Caterpillar or Chocolate Teapot? Top up the disk space for Windows 10 to find out
articles.content: Today's bit of signage silage is either Windows 10 protesting that it is not part of London's Oxford Street pedestrianization, or someone failing to heed an alert before the public is made all too aware that things aren't going well… Eagle-eyed Register reader Aaron Colwill spotted the sign outside the food hall entrance of a Marks & Spencer store on London's Oxford Street. It usually entices passersby through the doors with promises of treats inside, but today it appears to require a different kind of feeding. Disk space is running low. Marks and Spencer (also known as M&S and Marks and Sparks) is no stranger to cyber whoopsies , having been the victim of an attack in 2025 in which crooks made off with customer data. Later that year, it reckoned cleanup costs would be about £136 million. That's quite a lot, but not enough to buy a bigger hard disk for Windows 10, it seems. Storage prices have increased over the years, but surely not that much? Colwill reckoned that Windows 10 21H2 LTSC was behind the problems. It could well be. While support for 21H2 ended for many users in 2023, Windows 10 LTSC 2021 will carry on until Jan 12, 2027, meaning engineers might have an exciting festive period ahead of them. Windows 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC 2021 will receive extended support until Jan 13, 2032. Either way, using Windows to advertise the Food Hall's wares seems slightly overkill. Simple posters, for example, never run out of disk space or attract the bork fairy's attention. Perhaps they might use something that lacks the voracious appetite for storage that Microsoft's finest demands. According to the Windows biz, installing Windows 10 requires at least 32 GB of disk space, ideally more. It all seems a bit excessive for a cake-based caterpillar advert. Then again, when your operating system tends to have the resilience of a chocolate teapot, using it to advertise a chocolate insect might not be such a bad idea after all. ®
